units.evidence: We're closed.

units.claim: Tremaine bribed the clerk to find information on Bram.
units.evidence: A folded bill opened on the counter. The thin man's eyes darted toward it. His hand eased out, covered the bill. He grinned quickly.

units.claim: Bram bought the property on May 19, 1901.
units.evidence: May 19. Acreage sold, One Dollar and other G&V consid. NW Quarter Section 24, Township Elsby. Bram. (see Vol. 9 & cet.)

units.claim: Tremaine did not reveal the reason for his inquiry about Bram.
units.evidence: No. No trouble.

units.claim: Acreage was sold for One Dollar and other G&V considerations.
units.evidence: Acreage sold, One Dollar and other G&V consid.

units.claim: The sold acreage is the NW Quarter Section 24, Township Elsby.
units.evidence: NW Quarter Section 24, Township Elsby.

units.claim: Bram purchased the land.
units.evidence: Bram.

units.claim: The transaction occurred on May 19th.
units.evidence: May 19.

units.claim: Tremaine asked for the translation of the ledger entry.
units.evidence: "Translated, what does that mean?" said Tremaine.

units.claim: The ledger entry refers to Bram buying a quarter section on May 19th, 1901.
units.evidence: That's the ledger for 1901; means Bram bought a quarter section on the nineteenth of May.

units.claim: Tremaine did not want the clerk to look up the deed.
units.evidence: "No, thanks," Tremaine said. "That's all I needed."

units.claim: The clerk thought Bram must be nearly ninety years old.
units.evidence: Nineteen-oh-one, he said. "I never thought of it before, but you know, old Bram must be dern near to ninety years old. Spry for that age."

units.claim: There are superstitions about Bram's place being haunted.
units.evidence: Lots of funny stories about old Bram. Useta say his place was haunted. You know; funny noises and lights.

units.claim: People believed there was money buried at Bram's place.
units.evidence: And they used to say there was money buried out at his place.

units.claim: The clerk claimed nobody in town has ever seen Bram between sundown and sunup.
units.evidence: Nobody in this town's ever seen Bram between sundown and sunup.

units.claim: Tremaine visited the Elsby Public Library.
units.evidence: Inside, Tremaine followed a paper-dry woman of indeterminate age to a rack of yellowed newsprint.

units.claim: The librarian warned Tremaine to handle the old papers carefully.
units.evidence: You have to handle these old papers carefully.

units.claim: Tremaine wanted to see the newspaper from May 19, 1901.
units.evidence: I want nineteen-oh-one, if they go back that far.

units.claim: The newspaper article mentioned Bram purchasing a quarter section of land north of town.
units.evidence: Mr. Bram has purchased a quarter section of fine grazing land, north of town, together with a sturdy house, from J. P. Spivey of Elsby.

units.claim: Bram was a newcomer to the county and had been living at Mrs. Stoate's Guest Home.
units.evidence: Mr. Bram, who is a newcomer to the county, has been a resident of Mrs. Stoate's Guest Home in Elsby for the past months.

units.claim: Tremaine requested to see earlier issues of the newspaper from around the start of the year.
units.evidence: "May I see some earlier issues; from about the first of the year?"

units.claim: A severe thunderstorm occurred on the night of July 5, 1900, causing a fire in the pine woods north of Spivey's farm.
units.evidence: A Severe Thunderstorm. Citizens of Elsby and the country were much alarmed by a violent cloudburst, accompanied by lightning and thunder, during the night of the fifth. A fire set in the pine woods north of Spivey's farm destroyed a considerable amount of timber and threatened the house before burning itself out along the river.

units.claim: The librarian informed Tremaine that the library had to close.
units.evidence: The librarian was at Tremaine's side. "I have to close the library now. You'll have to come back tomorrow."

units.claim: Tremaine noticed a black late-model sedan with a heavy antenna pass by him.
units.evidence: A block away a black late-model sedan rounded a corner with a faint squeal of tires and gunned past him, a heavy antenna mounted forward of the left rear tail fin whipping in the slipstream.

units.claim: Tremaine chased after the police car.
units.evidence: Tremaine set off at a run, covered the two blocks to the hotel, yanked open the door to his car, slid into the seat, made a U-turn, and headed north after the police car.

units.claim: Tremaine found the police car parked on the shoulder of the highway north of Elsby.
units.evidence: Two miles into the dark hills north of the Elsby city limits, Tremaine rounded a curve. The police car was parked on the shoulder beside the highway just ahead.

units.claim: Tremaine identified himself to the police officer as someone from Washington.
units.evidence: "Oh," said the cop, "you're the big shot from Washington."

units.claim: Tremaine communicated with Grammond, the State Police chief, via the car set.
units.evidence: He turned and spoke to the other cop, who muttered into the mike before handing it to Tremaine.

units.claim: Tremaine expressed concern about the police presence in Elsby.
units.evidence: I thought you were going to keep your men away from Elsby until I gave the word, Grammond.

units.claim: Grammond was upset about not being informed about the Elsby angle.
units.evidence: That was before I knew your Washington stuffed shirts were holding out on me.

units.claim: Tremaine confirmed that the police presence might influence their investigation.
units.evidence: It's nothing we can go to court with, Grammond. And the job you were doing might have been influenced if I'd told you about the Elsby angle.

units.claim: Grammond was frustrated about not being able to search the town thoroughly.
units.evidence: Grammond cursed. "I could have put my men in the town and taken it apart brick by brick in the time—"

units.claim: Tremaine stated that he didn't want the suspect to go underground due to police presence.
units.evidence: That's just what I don't want. If our bird sees cops cruising, he'll go underground.

units.claim: Grammond felt undervalued by Tremaine's team.
units.evidence: You've got it all figured, I see. I'm just the dumb hick you boys use for the spade work, that it?

units.claim: Tremaine received the confirmation he needed from Grammond.
units.evidence: Pull your lip back in. You've given me the confirmation I needed.

units.claim: Grammond was uncertain about the source of the signal.
units.evidence: For all I know, it's forty midgets on bicycles, pedalling all over the damned state.

units.claim: Grammond expressed frustration about being used for manual labor.
units.evidence: You've got it all figured, I see. I'm just the dumb hick you boys use for the spade work, that it?

units.claim: Grammond believes someone is sending a signal.
units.evidence: All I know is that somebody somewhere is punching out a signal.

units.claim: Tremaine stated that the smallest hyperwave transmitter known to the US government weighs three tons.
units.evidence: The smallest hyperwave transmitter Uncle Sam knows how to build weighs three tons,

units.claim: Grammond is unwilling to be excluded from the operation.
units.evidence: It looks like Grammond's not willing to be left out in the cold, Fred.

units.claim: Fred suggests that Grammond might have a valid point.
units.evidence: I don't know but what he might have something,

units.claim: Tremaine believes they are not dealing with simple criminals.
units.evidence: We're not dealing with West Virginia moonshiners.

units.claim: Fred asserts his authority over the investigation.
units.evidence: Don't tell me my job, Tremaine!

units.claim: Tremaine drinks Scotch before leaving the hotel.
units.evidence: He tossed it down, then pulled on his coat and left the hotel.

units.claim: Tremaine visits a three-story mansion in Elsby.
units.evidence: Number 89 was a once-stately three-storied mansion overgrown with untrimmed vines, its windows squares of sad yellow light.

units.claim: Miss Carroll is around eighty years old.
units.evidence: Only a faint quaver reflected her age—close to eighty, Tremaine thought, startled.

units.claim: Miss Carroll remembers Tremaine from his youth.
units.evidence: There is nothing whatever wrong with my faculties, James,

units.claim: Miss Carroll believes Tremaine has succeeded in life.
units.evidence: You look very well, James, she said, nodding. I'm pleased to see that you've amounted to something.

units.claim: Miss Carroll thinks Tremaine made a wise decision to leave Elsby.
units.evidence: You were wise to leave Elsby. There is no future here for a young man.

units.claim: Tremaine seeks information about Mr. Bram.
units.evidence: How long has Mr. Bram lived in Elsby?

units.claim: Miss Carroll is uncertain about the year Mr. Bram moved to Elsby.
units.evidence: Mr. Bram came here when I was a young woman. I'm not certain of the year.

units.claim: Miss Carroll does not know what Mr. Bram does for a living.
units.evidence: What does he do for a living? I have no idea.

units.claim: Miss Carroll is unsure why Mr. Bram settled in Elsby.
units.evidence: Why did a healthy young fellow like Bram settle out in that isolated piece of country? What's his story? I'm ... not sure that anyone truly knows Bram's story.

units.claim: Mr. Bram's only name is Bram.
units.evidence: That is his only name. Just ... Bram.

units.claim: Miss Carroll once had a relationship with Bram.
units.evidence: Many years ago I was courted by Bram.

units.claim: Bram told Miss Carroll about fighting evil beings in a cave.
units.evidence: He said that each night he fought a battle with evil beings, alone, in a cave beneath his house.

units.claim: Bram gave Miss Carroll a locket with a secret mechanism.
units.evidence: He took a locket from his neck and put it into my hand. He told me to keep it and, if ever I should need him, to press it between my fingers in a secret way ... and he would come.

units.claim: Miss Carroll still possesses the locket.
units.evidence: She handed the locket to him. It was heavy, smooth.

units.claim: Miss Carroll allows Tremaine to take the locket with him.
units.evidence: Miss Carroll nodded.

units.claim: Tremaine asks if Miss Carroll still has the locket.
units.evidence: "This locket," said Tremaine, "do you still have it?"

units.claim: Miss Carroll hesitates before showing Tremaine the locket.
units.evidence: Miss Carroll hesitated, then put her hand to her throat, lifted a silver disc on a fine golden chain.

units.claim: Miss Carroll refers to herself as a foolish old woman.
units.evidence: "You see what a foolish old woman I am, James."

units.claim: Tremaine requests to see the locket.
units.evidence: "May I see it?"

units.claim: Miss Carroll hands the locket to Tremaine.
units.evidence: She handed the locket to him.

units.claim: Tremaine describes the locket as heavy and smooth.
units.evidence: It was heavy, smooth.

units.claim: Tremaine asks permission to take the locket with him.
units.evidence: "I'd like to examine this more closely," he said. "May I take it with me?"

units.claim: Miss Carroll nods in agreement to let Tremaine take the locket.
units.evidence: Miss Carroll nodded.

units.claim: Miss Carroll mentions another thing that may be meaningless.
units.evidence: "There is one other thing," she said, "perhaps quite meaningless...."

units.claim: Tremaine expresses gratitude for any lead.
units.evidence: "I'd be grateful for any lead."

units.claim: Miss Carroll mentions that Bram fears the thunder.
units.evidence: "Bram fears the thunder."

units.claim: Tremaine walks towards the main street of Elsby.
units.evidence: As Tremaine walked slowly toward the lighted main street of Elsby

units.claim: A car stops beside Tremaine.
units.evidence: a car pulled to a stop beside him.

units.claim: Jess leans out of the car and asks Tremaine if he had any luck.
units.evidence: Jess leaned out, peered at Tremaine and asked: "Any luck, Jimmy?"

units.claim: Tremaine shakes his head indicating he is not making progress.
units.evidence: Tremaine shook his head. "I'm getting nowhere fast. The Bram idea's a dud, I'm afraid."

units.claim: Jess suggests going to check on Bram.
units.evidence: "Funny thing about Bram. You know, he hasn't showed up yet. I'm getting a little worried. Want to run out there with me and take a look around?"

units.claim: Tremaine agrees to go with Jess but wants to be back by full dark.
units.evidence: "Sure. Just so I'm back by full dark."

units.claim: Jess asks Tremaine about State Police being involved.
units.evidence: "Jimmy, what's this about State Police nosing around here? I thought you were playing a lone hand from what you were saying to me."

units.claim: Tremaine explains that Grammond might be ahead of him.
units.evidence: "I thought so too, Jess. But it looks like Grammond's a jump ahead of me. He smells headlines in this; he doesn't want to be left out."

units.claim: Jess thinks State Police could be helpful.
units.evidence: "Well, the State cops could be mighty handy to have around. I'm wondering why you don't want 'em in. If there's some kind of spy ring working—"

units.claim: Tremaine believes they are up against an unknown quantity.
units.evidence: "We're up against an unknown quantity. I don't know what's behind this and neither does anybody else."

units.claim: Tremaine feels they have made enough mistakes in recent years.
units.evidence: "Maybe it's a ring of Bolsheviks ... and maybe it's something bigger. I have the feeling we've made enough mistakes in the last few years; I don't want to see this botched."

units.claim: Jess and Tremaine arrive at Bram's house as the sun sets.
units.evidence: The last pink light of sunset was fading from the clouds to the west as Jess swung the car through the open gate, pulled up under the old trees before the square-built house.

units.claim: The windows of Bram's house are dark.
units.evidence: The windows were dark.

units.claim: Jess and Tremaine circle the house and notice a black patch of charred flooring under a window.
units.evidence: There was a black patch of charred flooring under the window, and the paint on the wall above it was bubbled.

units.claim: Jess finds an empty shotgun shell outside the house.
units.evidence: Jess leaned down, picked up an empty shotgun shell.

units.claim: Jess tries the door and it opens revealing a broken hasp.
units.evidence: He tried the door. It opened. A broken hasp dangled.

units.claim: Jess and Tremaine enter the house which is silent and deserted.
units.evidence: The two men got out, circled the house once, then mounted the steps and rapped on the door. ... It was silent, deserted.

units.claim: In the kitchen, Jess uses a flashlight and notices an empty plate on the table.
units.evidence: In the kitchen Jess flicked the beam of his flashlight around the room. An empty plate lay on the oilcloth-covered table.

units.claim: Jess concludes the place is empty.
units.evidence: "This place is empty," he said. "Anybody'd think he'd been gone a week."

units.claim: A distant yelp is heard.
units.evidence: A thin yelp sounded in the distance.

units.claim: Jess assumes the sound is from a dog.
units.evidence: "Dern hounddog, I guess."

units.claim: A low growl is heard.
units.evidence: A low growl seemed to rumble distantly.

units.claim: Jess and Tremaine notice a spatter of dark droplets on the floor.
units.evidence: Jess shone the light on the floor. "Look here," he said. The ring of light showed a spatter of dark droplets all across the plank floor.

units.claim: Tremaine identifies the droplets as blood.
units.evidence: "That's blood, Jess...."

units.claim: Tremaine follows the trail of blood.
units.evidence: Tremaine followed the line of drops across the floor.

units.claim: A wail is heard, trailing off into silence.
units.evidence: A wail sounded, a thin forlorn cry, trailing off into silence.

units.claim: Jess doubts the presence of supernatural beings.
units.evidence: "I'm too damned old to start believing in spooks," he said.

units.claim: Tremaine suggests asking Hull Gaskin questions.
units.evidence: I think." Tremaine said, "that we'd better go ask Hull Gaskin a few questions."

units.claim: Hull Gaskin is in a cell at the police station.
units.evidence: At the station Jess led Tremaine to a cell where a lanky teen-age boy lounged on a steel-framed cot, blinking up at the visitor under a mop of greased hair.

units.claim: Jess introduces Tremaine to Hull Gaskin.
units.evidence: "Hull, this is Mr. Tremaine," said Jess.

units.claim: Hull Gaskin claims he has not done anything wrong.
units.evidence: "I ain't done nothin," Hull said sullenly.

units.claim: Hull Gaskin mentions burning a Communist.
units.evidence: "There ain't nothin wrong with burnin out a Commie, is there?"

units.claim: Hull Gaskin refers to Bram as a Communist.
units.evidence: "Bram's a Commie, is he?"

units.claim: Hull Gaskin justifies his statement based on Bram being a foreigner.
units.evidence: "He's a foreigner, ain't he?" the youth shot back.

units.claim: Hull Gaskin mentions hearing about the search for spies.
units.evidence: "Besides, we heard...."

units.claim: Hull Gaskin mentions that police were talking about spies.
units.evidence: "Cops was talkin about 'em," he said.

units.claim: Hull Gaskin mentions police questioning him about suspicious people.
units.evidence: They parked out east of town, on 302, back of the woodlot. They called me over and asked me a bunch of questions. Said I could help 'em get them spies. Wanted to know all about any funny-actin people around hers.

units.claim: Hull Gaskin mentions mentioning Bram to the police.
units.evidence: The boy darted another look at Tremaine. "They said they figured the spies was out north of town. Well, Bram's a foreigner, and he's out that way, ain't he?"

units.claim: The ancient rule was to either survive or perish on a planet without spaceflight.
units.evidence: The ancient rule was sink or swim—swim in the miasma of a planet without spaceflight, or sink to utter destruction!

units.claim: The story was originally published in Worlds of If Science Fiction, July 1963.
units.evidence: This etext was produced from Worlds of If Science Fiction, July 1963.

units.claim: The narrator and others are preparing to board a scoutship.
units.evidence: The horses and packs were loaded before we went aboard the scoutship.

units.claim: The scout bay is described as a large airlock with multiple small ships.
units.evidence: The scout bay is no more than a great oversized airlock with a dozen small ships squatting over their tubes

units.claim: There are sixteen girls and thirteen boys preparing for the journey.
units.evidence: There were sixteen of us girls and thirteen boys.

units.claim: Jimmy Dentremont offers to be Mia's partner on the planet.
units.evidence: "Mia, do you want to go partners if we can get together when we get down?"

units.claim: Mia rejects Jimmy's offer due to a previous argument.
units.evidence: "Not likely. I want to come back alive."

units.claim: Mia's name is Mia Havero and she is fourteen years old.
units.evidence: My name is Mia Havero. I'm fourteen, of course, or I wouldn't be telling this.

units.claim: Mia is short, dark, and scrawny.
units.evidence: I'm short, dark and scrawny, though I don't expect that scrawniness to last much longer.

units.claim: George Fuhonin is the pilot of the scoutship.
units.evidence: After we were all settled, George Fuhonin, the pilot, raised the ramps.

units.claim: The scoutship drops the passengers onto the planet after depressurizing the tube.
units.evidence: We sat there for five minutes while they bled air out of our tube and then we just ... dropped.

units.claim: The planet Tintera was last contacted almost 150 years ago.
units.evidence: The last contact the Ship had had with it—and we were the ones who dropped them—was almost 150 years ago.

units.claim: Mia's father is the Chairman of the Council.
units.evidence: I wouldn't have known that much if Daddy weren't Chairman of the Council.

units.claim: Mia feels uncomfortable on planets due to gravity issues and other factors.
units.evidence: Planets make me feel wretched. The gravity is always wrong, for one thing.

units.claim: The scoutship drops the passengers over a sea and then over gray-green forested hills.
units.evidence: We swung over the sea from the morning side and then dropped low over gray-green forested hills.

units.claim: Jimmy Dentremont jumps down the ramp first.
units.evidence: Jimmy D. jumped up, grabbed his gear and then led his horse down the ramp.

units.claim: The scoutship returns to pick up the passengers after a month.
units.evidence: When we turn fourteen, they drop us on the nearest colonized planet and come back one month later.

units.claim: The narrator checks her gear including a sonic pistol, pickup signal, saddle, cinches, food, and clothes.
units.evidence: I began to check my gear out—sonic pistol, pickup signal so I could be found at the end of the month, saddle and cinches, food and clothes.

units.claim: Venie Morlock has a crush on Jimmy Dentremont.
units.evidence: Venie Morlock has got a crush on Jimmy D.

units.claim: The first night on the planet is difficult for Mia due to loneliness and darkness.
units.evidence: The first night was hell, I guess because I'm not used to having the lights out.

units.claim: Horst doubts that a Losel would notice the small boy.
units.evidence: He be awfully small, Horst. I doubt me a Losel'd even notice him at all.

units.claim: The rider expected the boy to dissolve in terror.
units.evidence: The rider looked at me. When I didn't dissolve in terror as he expected, he shrugged and one of the other men laughed.

units.claim: The hard man decided the boy would ride to Forton for protection.
units.evidence: This boy will be riding along with us to Forton for protection.

units.claim: The boy felt uncomfortable looking at the creatures being driven along.
units.evidence: I looked down at the plodding, unhappy creatures they were driving along and one looked back at me with dull, expressionless golden eyes. I felt uncomfortable.

units.claim: The boy refused to ride along with the men.
units.evidence: I said, 'I don't think so.'

units.claim: The man insisted the boy would ride along with them.
units.evidence: He said, 'I do think so,' and reached for the rifle in his saddle boot.

units.claim: The boy whipped out a sonic pistol.
units.evidence: I whipped my sonic pistol out so fast that he was caught leaning over with the rifle half out.

units.claim: The man was surprised by the boy's action.
units.evidence: His jaw dropped. He knew what I held and he didn't want to be fried.

units.claim: The boy ordered the men to drop their rifles.
units.evidence: I said, 'Ease your rifles out and drop them gently to the ground.'

units.claim: The men complied and dropped their rifles.
units.evidence: They did, watching me all the while with wary expressions.

units.claim: The boy offered to let the men retrieve their rifles.
units.evidence: I said, 'If you want your rifles, you can go back and get them now.'

units.claim: One of the men retreated to get the rifles.
units.evidence: At the next bend I looked back and saw four of them holding their packhorses and the creatures still while one beat a dust-raising retreat down the road.

units.claim: The boy felt good after the encounter.
units.evidence: I put this episode in the 'file and hold for analysis' section in my mind and rode on, feeling good.

units.claim: The boy rode through a valley with farms and fields.
units.evidence: The country leveled into a great rolling valley and the trees gave way to great farms and fields.

units.claim: Green creatures were working in the fields.
units.evidence: In the fields, working, were some of the green creatures, which surprised me since the ones I'd seen before hadn't seemed smart enough to count to one, let alone do any work.

units.claim: The boy encountered people on horseback and trucks.
units.evidence: I met people on horseback, and twice I met trucks moving silently past.

units.claim: The boy passed a wagon driven by an elderly man.
units.evidence: And I overtook a wagon driven by the oldest man I've seen in my life.

units.claim: The boy entered a town with outdated buildings.
units.evidence: The town was all stone, wood and brick. Out of date. Out of time, really.

units.claim: There were no machines more complex than trucks in the town.
units.evidence: There were no machines more complicated than the trucks I'd seen earlier.

units.claim: The town had a newspaper office with a headline about invasion.
units.evidence: At the edge of town, I passed a newspaper office with a headline pasted in the window—INVASION!

units.claim: The town lacked girls over ten years old and grown-up women.
units.evidence: In all that town, I didn't see one girl over ten years old and no grown-up women at all.

units.claim: The boy noticed many children in the town.
units.evidence: It was the most foul thing I've ever seen. It struck me then—these people were Free Birthers!

units.claim: The boy felt nauseous upon seeing the families in the town.
units.evidence: I felt a wave of nausea and I closed my eyes until it passed.

units.claim: The boy learned about the history of Earth's destruction due to overpopulation.
units.evidence: The first thing you learn in school is that if it weren't for idiot and criminal people like these, Earth would never have been destroyed.

units.claim: The boy's ancestors had foresight to evacuate Earth.
units.evidence: My great-great-grandparents were among those who had enough foresight to see what was coming.

units.claim: The boy felt frightened by the situation on Tintera.
units.evidence: For the first time since I landed on Tintera, I felt really frightened.

units.claim: The boy wished for Jimmy D's help.
units.evidence: I couldn't help wishing for Jimmy D. Whatever else he is, he's smart and brains I needed.

units.claim: The boy considered finding a library to gather information.
units.evidence: The best thing I could think of was to find a library, but that might be a job.

units.claim: The ship lifted away from Ninc and the narrator like a rising bird.
units.evidence: The ship lifted impersonally away from Ninc and me like a rising bird,

units.claim: The ship's gray-blue color was similar to the half-overcast sky.
units.evidence: Its gray-blue color was almost the color of the half-overcast sky,

units.claim: The narrator was unsure when they last saw the ship.
units.evidence: so I was never sure when I saw it last.

units.claim: The first night without lights was difficult for the narrator.
units.evidence: The first night was hell, I guess because I'm not used to having the lights out.

units.claim: Being alone in the dark made the narrator feel lonely.
units.evidence: That's when you really start to feel lonely, being alone in the dark.

units.claim: The narrator rode in a spiral search pattern for two days.
units.evidence: I rode in a spiral search pattern during the next two days.

units.claim: The narrator's goals were to stay alive, find people, and find others.
units.evidence: I had three things in mind—stay alive, find people and find some of the others.

units.claim: The narrator did not want to join forces with Jimmy D.
units.evidence: The third was to join forces, though not with that meatball Jimmy D.

units.claim: The narrator and Jimmy D often fought due to their stubbornness.
units.evidence: The trouble is that I don't take nothing from nobody, especially him, and he doesn't take nothing from nobody, especially me. So we do a lot of fighting.

units.claim: The narrator had a good month for Trial.
units.evidence: I had a good month for Trial.

units.claim: The narrator's birthday is in November.
units.evidence: My birthday is in November

units.claim: The narrator preferred spring on Tintera to December on the Ship.
units.evidence: It was spring on Tintera, but it was December in the Ship,

units.claim: After returning, the narrator celebrated five days of Holiday.
units.evidence: and after we got back we had five days of Holiday to celebrate.

units.claim: During two days of riding, the narrator encountered only a few odd-looking animals.
units.evidence: In two days of riding, I ran onto nothing but a few odd-looking animals.

units.claim: The narrator shot and ate a small animal that tasted good.
units.evidence: I shot one small one and ate it. It turned out to taste pretty good,

units.claim: The narrator compared the taste of the small animal to Hambone No. 4.
units.evidence: though not as good as a slice from Hambone No. 4, to my mind the best meat vat on the Ship.

units.claim: The narrator found a narrow road made of sand over a hard base.
units.evidence: It was narrow and made of sand spread over a hard base.

units.claim: The road had tracks of horses and both narrow and wide wheels.
units.evidence: Out of the marks in the sand, I could pick out the tracks of horses and both narrow and wide wheels.

units.claim: Horses were included in the evacuation plan for the colonies.
units.evidence: One of the smartest moves in history was to include horses when they dropped the colonies.

units.claim: The evacuation plan originated with the whole evac plan back on Earth.
units.evidence: I say "they" because, while we did the actual dropping, the idea originated with the whole evac plan back on Earth.

units.claim: The first Great Ship was completed in 2025.
units.evidence: The first of the Great Ships was finished in 2025.

units.claim: Eight ships were built by 2041.
units.evidence: One of the eight, as well as the two that were being built then, went up with everything else in the Solar System in 2041.

units.claim: 112 colonies were planted in 16 years.
units.evidence: In that sixteen years 112 colonies were planted.

units.claim: The narrator traveled east on the road.
units.evidence: We'd come in from the west over the ocean, so I traveled east on the road.

units.claim: The narrator encountered five men on horseback herding ugly creatures.
units.evidence: I came on my first travelers three hours later. I rounded a tree-lined bend, ducking an overhanging branch, and pulled Ninc to a stop. There were five men on horseback herding a bunch of the ugliest creatures alive.

units.claim: The creatures were green, squat-bodied, and had long limbs and knobby bulges at their joints.
units.evidence: They were green and grotesque. They had squat bodies, long limbs and knobby bulges at their joints.

units.claim: The creatures had square, flat animal masks for faces.
units.evidence: They had square, flat animal masks for faces.

units.claim: The creatures walked on their hind legs and had paws that were almost hands.
units.evidence: But they walked on their hind legs and they had paws that were almost hands,

units.claim: The creatures made a wordless, chilling, lowing sound.
units.evidence: They made a wordless, chilling, lowing sound as they milled and plodded along.

units.claim: The leader of the group was a middle-aged, large man with a hard face.
units.evidence: He was a middle-aged man, maybe as old as my Daddy. He was large and he had a hard face.

units.claim: The leader warned the narrator about escaped Losels in the woods.
units.evidence: "What be you doing out here, boy? Be you out of your head? There be escaped Losels in these woods."

units.claim: The leader suggested the narrator ride with them for protection.
units.evidence: "Maybe you'd better ride on from here with us. For protection."

units.claim: The leader had an odd way of speaking.
units.evidence: He had an odd way of twisting his sounds, almost as though he had a mouthful of mush.

units.claim: Another rider suggested the narrator might not need protection.
units.evidence: He be awfully small, Horst. I doubt me a Losel'd even notice him at all. We mought as well throw him back again.

units.claim: The leader decided the narrator would ride with them to Forton for protection.
units.evidence: This boy will be riding along with us to Forton for protection.

units.claim: The narrator felt uncomfortable looking at the creatures.
units.evidence: I looked down at the plodding, unhappy creatures they were driving along and one looked back at me with dull, expressionless golden eyes. I felt uncomfortable.

units.claim: The narrator refused to ride with the group.
units.evidence: I said, "I don't think so."

units.claim: He stopped dragging the narrator and dropped him in a heap.
units.evidence: he stopped dragging me and dropped me in a heap.

units.claim: The narrator was threatened with harm if he made any noise.
units.evidence: "Make any noise," he said, "and I'll hurt you."

units.claim: There was enough moonlight for the man to examine his hand.
units.evidence: There was enough moonlight for that.

units.claim: The man considered clubbing the narrator.
units.evidence: "I ought to club you anyway," he said.

units.claim: Another person came up after the narrator dropped the saddle.
units.evidence: The one I'd dropped the saddle on came up then.

units.claim: Others were putting the animals in the pen.
units.evidence: The others were putting the animals in the pen.

units.claim: Jack was stopped from kicking the narrator by Horst.
units.evidence: He started to kick me, but Horst stopped him.

units.claim: Horst instructed to look through the narrator's gear and bring the horse and usable items.
units.evidence: "No," he said. "Look through the kid's gear, bring the horse and what we can use."

units.claim: Jack hesitated to follow Horst's order.
units.evidence: The other one didn't move.

units.claim: Horst used a menacing tone to urge Jack to follow orders.
units.evidence: "Get going, Jack," he said in a menacing tone

units.claim: Horst established dominance over who gets to kick in his group.
units.evidence: It seemed to me that Horst wasn't so much objecting to me being kicked, but was rather establishing who did the kicking in his bunch.

units.claim: The narrator was scared but still had a pistol under his jacket.
units.evidence: I was scared, but I still had the pistol under my jacket.

units.claim: The narrator told Horst that he couldn't do what he was doing and get away with it.
units.evidence: You can't do this and get away with it.

units.claim: Horst warned the narrator not to give him a hard time.
units.evidence: So don't give me a hard time.

units.claim: Horst still thought the narrator was a boy.
units.evidence: He still thought I was a boy.

units.claim: The narrator mentioned that the courts wouldn't let Horst get away with what he was doing.
units.evidence: The courts won't let you get away with this

units.claim: Horst laughed at the narrator's mention of the courts.
units.evidence: He laughed, not a phony, villian-type laugh, but a real laugh

units.claim: Horst claimed he was doing the narrator a favor by letting him go.
units.evidence: I be doing you a favor. I be taking what I can use of your gear, but I be letting you go.

units.claim: Horst stated that going to court would result in the narrator being locked up and losing everything.
units.evidence: You go to court and they'll take everything and lock you up besides.

units.claim: Horst mentioned that the narrator shouting he was off one of the Ships was enough reason for trouble.
units.evidence: Every time you open your mouth you shout that you be off one of the Ships

units.claim: Horst mentioned that there was already one of the narrator's kind in jail in Forton.
units.evidence: They already have one of you brats in jail in Forton.

units.claim: Jack brought Ninc with the narrator's stuff loaded on.
units.evidence: up came Jack leading Ninc, with all my stuff loaded on.

units.claim: Jack couldn't figure out what the pickup signal was for.
units.evidence: I can't make out what this be for.

units.claim: Horst instructed to throw away the pickup signal.
units.evidence: Throw it away

units.claim: The narrator aimed his gun at Horst and demanded the pickup signal.
units.evidence: I leveled my gun at them—I said, "Hand that over to me."

units.claim: Horst expressed disgust at the narrator's action.
units.evidence: Horst made a disgusted sound.

units.claim: The narrator threatened to fry Horst if he made any noise.
units.evidence: Don't make any noise, or you'll fry.

units.claim: The narrator asked about the name of the kid in jail in Forton.
units.evidence: What's the name of the kid in jail in Forton.

units.claim: Horst couldn't immediately recall the name of the kid in jail in Forton.
units.evidence: I can't remember

units.claim: The narrator's arm was hit and the gun went flying.
units.evidence: my arm was hit a numbing blow from behind and the gun went flying.

units.claim: Jack pounced after the narrator's gun.
units.evidence: Jack pounced after it

units.claim: Horst stomped on the pickup signal until it cracked and fell apart.
units.evidence: He dropped it on the ground and said in a voice far colder than mine could ever be, because it was natural and mine wasn't, "The piece be yours." Then he tromped on it until it cracked and fell apart.

units.claim: Horst slapped the narrator hard.
units.evidence: He slapped me so hard that my ears rang.

units.claim: The narrator called Horst a big louse.
units.evidence: You big louse.

units.claim: Horst punched the narrator in the face.
units.evidence: All I can remember is a flash of pain as his fist crunched against the side of my face and then nothing.

units.claim: He ran for almost a mile before being pulled down to a walk.
units.evidence: I let him run for almost a mile before I pulled him down to a walk

units.claim: The speaker wishes for Jimmy D.
units.evidence: I couldn't help wishing for Jimmy D.

units.claim: Eavesdropping is a lousy method to find out what's going on.
units.evidence: How do you find out what's going on? Eavesdrop? That's a lousy method.

units.claim: People cannot be depended on to talk about desired topics.
units.evidence: For one thing, people can't be depended on to talk about the things you want to hear.

units.claim: Eavesdropping can lead to getting caught.
units.evidence: For another, you're likely to get caught.

units.claim: Asking someone for information can result in negative consequences.
units.evidence: Ask somebody? Who? Make the mistake of bracing a fellow like Horst and you might wind up with a sore head and an empty pocket.

units.claim: Finding a library is considered the best option but may be difficult.
units.evidence: The best thing I could think of was to find a library, but that might be a job.

units.claim: The speaker had experienced two bad shocks on that day.
units.evidence: I'd had two bad shocks on this day, but they weren't the last.

units.claim: In the late afternoon, the sun was starting to sink and a cool wind was starting to ripple the tree leaves.
units.evidence: In the late afternoon, when the sun was starting to sink and a cool wind was starting to ripple the tree leaves,

units.claim: The speaker saw a scoutship high in the sky colored red by the dying sun.
units.evidence: I saw the scoutship high in the sky. The dying sun colored it a deep red.

units.claim: The speaker wondered what had gone wrong with the scoutship returning.
units.evidence: Back again? I wondered what had gone wrong.

units.claim: The speaker triggered a contact signal to the scoutship.
units.evidence: I reached down into my saddlebag and brought out my contact signal.

units.claim: The scoutship maneuvered in a familiar way associated with George Fuhonin.
units.evidence: The scoutship swung up in the sky in a familiar movement calculated to drop the stomach out of everybody aboard. George Fuhonin's style.

units.claim: The speaker was unsure why the scoutship returned but was not really sorry.
units.evidence: I didn't know why he was back, but I wasn't really sorry.

units.claim: The scoutship performed poorly, indicating it was not one of theirs.
units.evidence: Not too different, but not ours.

units.claim: The scoutship's return added to the speaker's sense of defeat and tiredness.
units.evidence: I felt defeated and tired.

units.claim: The speaker found a campsite with two wagons and two permanent buildings.
units.evidence: Not much farther along the road, I came to a campsite with two wagons pulled in for the night, and I couldn't help but pull in myself. The campsite was large and had two permanent buildings on it.

units.claim: One building was a well enclosure and the other was a high-walled pen without a roof.
units.evidence: One was a well enclosure and the other was little more than a high-walled pen. It didn't even have a roof.

units.claim: The speaker set up camp and ate dinner near a family with three children.
units.evidence: I set up camp and ate my dinner. In the wagon closest to me were a man, his wife and their three children.

units.claim: The children were playing near the high-walled pen.
units.evidence: The kids were running around and playing, and one of them ran close to the high-walled pen.

units.claim: The father pulled one child away from the high-walled pen.
units.evidence: His father came and pulled him away.

units.claim: The speaker did not respond to a child's greeting.
units.evidence: When one of them said hello to me, I didn't even answer.

units.claim: The speaker felt sympathy for children with multiple siblings.
units.evidence: Isn't that horrible?

units.claim: An old man with white hair arrived at the campsite.
units.evidence: About the time I finished eating, and before it grew dark, the old man I had seen earlier in the day drove his wagon in. He fascinated me. He had white hair, something I had read about in stories but had never seen before.

units.claim: At nightfall, a large fire was started and everyone gathered around.
units.evidence: When nightfall came, they started a large fire. Everybody gathered around.

units.claim: There was singing followed by storytelling.
units.evidence: There was singing for awhile, and then the father of the children tried to pack them off to bed. But they weren't ready to go, so the old man started telling them a story.

units.claim: The old man told a story about Baba Yaga and a little girl.
units.evidence: It was about an old witch named Baba Yaga who lived in the forest in a house that stood on chicken legs. She was the nasty stepmother of a nice little girl, and to get rid of the kid, she sent her on a phony errand into the deep dark woods at nightfall.

units.claim: The little girl had a handkerchief, a comb, and a pearl to help her.
units.evidence: All the little girl had to help her were the handkerchief, the comb and the pearl that she had inherited from her dear dead mother.

units.claim: The little girl defeated Baba Yaga and returned home safely.
units.evidence: But, as it turned out, they were just enough to defeat nasty old Baba Yaga and bring the girl safely home.

units.claim: The speaker wished for the same outcome for themselves.
units.evidence: I wished for the same for myself.

units.claim: A commotion occurred on the road at the edge of the camp.
units.evidence: There was a commotion on the road at the edge of the camp.

units.claim: Someone complained about a day like this one and blamed Horst.
units.evidence: I'll be damned if I'll take another day like this one, Horst. We should have been here hours ago. It be your fault we're not.

units.claim: Horst growled a retort.
units.evidence: Horst growled a retort.

units.claim: The speaker decided to leave the campfire.
units.evidence: I decided that it was time for me to leave the campfire.

units.claim: The speaker packed up their belongings and moved towards Ninc.
units.evidence: I got up and eased away as Horst and his men came up to the fire, and cut back to where Ninc was parked. I grabbed up my blankets and mattress and started to roll them up.

units.claim: The speaker suspected the purpose of the high-walled pen.
units.evidence: I had a pretty good idea now what they used the high-walled pen for.

units.claim: The speaker intended to leave the campsite.
units.evidence: I should have known that they would have to pen the animals up for the night. I should have used my head. I hadn't and now it was time to take leave.

units.claim: The speaker was interrupted while trying to leave.
units.evidence: I never got the chance.

units.claim: Someone grabbed the speaker's shoulder and swung them around.
units.evidence: I was just heaving the saddle up on Ninc when I felt a hand on my shoulder and I was swung around.

units.claim: Horst and his men approached the speaker.
units.evidence: Well, well. Horst, look who we have here," he called. It was the one who'd made the joke about me being beneath the notice of a Losel. He was alone with me now, but with that call the others would be up fast.

units.claim: The speaker attacked the man who grabbed them.
units.evidence: I brought the saddle around as hard as I could and then up, and he went down. He started to get up again, so I dropped the saddle on him and reached inside my jacket for my gun.

units.claim: Someone grabbed the speaker from behind and pinned their arms.
units.evidence: Somebody grabbed me then from behind and pinned my arms to my side.

units.claim: The speaker attempted to scream but was prevented.
units.evidence: I opened my mouth to scream—I have a good scream—but a rough smelly hand clamped down over it before I had a chance to get more than a lungful of air.

units.claim: The speaker bit the hand covering their mouth.
units.evidence: I bit down hard—5000 lbs. psi, I'm told—but he didn't let me go.

units.claim: The speaker started kicking but was dragged off by Horst.
units.evidence: I started to kick, but Horst jerked me off my feet and dragged me off.

units.claim: Horst warned the speaker against making noise.
units.evidence: "Make any noise," he said, "and I'll hurt you."

units.claim: Horst examined his hand under moonlight.
units.evidence: He examined his hand. There was enough moonlight for that.

units.claim: Horst considered clubbing the speaker.
units.evidence: "I ought to club you anyway," he said.

units.claim: Another man came up to the speaker and was stopped from kicking them by Horst.
units.evidence: The one I'd dropped the saddle on came up then. The others were putting the animals in the pen. He started to kick me, but Horst stopped him.

units.claim: Casey Ritter is someone who never turns down a dare.
units.evidence: Casey Ritter, the guy who never turned down a dare

units.claim: Casey Ritter headed towards Jupiter's Great Red Spot.
units.evidence: headed in toward the great red spot of terrible Jupiter.

units.claim: Methane and ammonia planets are considered the dead-end of creation.
units.evidence: Those methane and ammonia planets, take it from me, they're the dead-end of creation

units.claim: Casey Ritter smuggled Kooleen crystals from Mars.
units.evidence: A man can get himself backed into a corner in this little old solar system. It just ain't big enough for a gent of scope and talent; and the day the Solar System Customs caught me red-handed smuggling Kooleen crystals in from Mars, I knew I was in that corner, and sewed up tight.

units.claim: Smuggling Kooleen crystals is illegal.
units.evidence: But—and this was the 'but' that was likely to deprive the System of my activities—even experimenting with them was illegal even if it needed to be done;

units.claim: Casey Ritter was not going to rat on his client.
units.evidence: Well, Casey Ritter may be a lot of things we won't mention, but he doesn't rat on his clients.

units.claim: Casey Ritter was sentenced to a trip to Jupiter instead of prison.
units.evidence: But they didn't foul me with this trip to good old Jupiter.

units.claim: Jupiter is considered worse than prison by Casey Ritter.
units.evidence: Jupiter was a death sentence.

units.claim: There are insect-like creatures inhabiting Jupiter's Red Spot.
units.evidence: Insect-like creatures who manifestly migrated there from some other system and who inhabit the Red Spot of the planet, floating in some kind of artificial anti-gravity field in the gaseous portion of the atmosphere—

units.claim: The government possesses authenticated photographs of the inhabitants of Jupiter's Red Spot.
units.evidence: We possess well-authenticated photographs of these inhabitants

units.claim: Casey Ritter was offered a pardon and a reward for visiting the inhabitants of Jupiter's Red Spot.
units.evidence: if you are prepared to visit them and in some way worm from them the secret of their anti-gravity field, the government stands ready to issue you a full pardon as well as a substantial monetary reward.

units.claim: The inhabitants of Jupiter's Red Spot resemble a cross between a scorpion and a grasshopper.
units.evidence: Well, a cross between a scorpion and a grasshopper, to be accurate.

units.claim: The inhabitants of Jupiter's Red Spot are approximately the size of a man.
units.evidence: About the size of a man, I believe.

units.claim: Casey Ritter refused the mission to Jupiter's Red Spot.
units.evidence: Take me to jail!

units.claim: Casey Ritter felt safer in prison than on the mission to Jupiter.
units.evidence: After all, in the pen a man can eat and breathe, and a guard won't reach in and nip off an arm or leg while he's got his back turned.

units.claim: Casey Ritter was placed in a cell after refusing the mission.
units.evidence: When I finally wore them down and got to my little cell, I looked around it with a feeling of real coziness.

units.claim: Casey Ritter was tricked into the mission by the government.
units.evidence: In plain English, I underestimated the enemy. Feeling safe and secure in the grip of the good old Iron College, I relaxed.

units.claim: A stoolie was planted on Casey Ritter during recreation.
units.evidence: At this strategic point, the enemy planted a stoolie on me. Not in my cell block. They were too smart for that. But we met at recreation, and his mug seemed familiar, like a wisp of smoke where no smoke has got a right to be;

units.claim: The enemy planted a stoolie on the narrator.
units.evidence: At this strategic point, the enemy planted a stoolie on me.

units.claim: The stoolie met the narrator during recreation.
units.evidence: But we met at recreation

units.claim: The stoolie's face seemed familiar to the narrator.
units.evidence: his mug seemed familiar

units.claim: The narrator had previously met Pard Hoskins in an asteroid real estate racket.
units.evidence: I'd met the shrimp before when I was wind up in an asteroid real estate racket.

units.claim: Pard Hoskins used the alias Pard Hoskins.
units.evidence: Pard Hoskins was his alias

units.claim: Pard Hoskins was known as a slick operator.
units.evidence: he had the tag of being a real slick operator

units.claim: Pard Hoskins was arrested for attempting to steal the Killicut Emeralds.
units.evidence: Oh, a pretty good jolt if they can keep hold of me... I just made a pass at the Killicut Emeralds, that's all, and got nabbed.

units.claim: The Killicut Emeralds are big as hen's eggs and flawless.
units.evidence: Big as hen's eggs, an even dozen of 'em; and flawless, I'm a-shoutin', not a flaw!

units.claim: The Killicut Emeralds are located in the inner shrine of the super-sacred, super-secret temple of the cavern-dwelling tribe of Killicuts on Mars.
units.evidence: Those emeralds were in the inner shrine of the super-sacred, super-secret temple of the cavern-dwelling tribe of Killicuts on Mars

units.claim: Pard Hoskins kept the method of his escape and hiding place of the emeralds a secret.
units.evidence: Sorry. Gotta keep that a secret. Likewise where I cached 'em.

units.claim: Pard Hoskins planned to sell the emeralds to Akroida on Jupiter.
units.evidence: When I chisel me way outa this squirrel cage, I'm gonna hit fer good old Jupe and sell 'em to Akroida.

units.claim: Akroida is the queen-scorp of the scorpions living on Jupiter.
units.evidence: Akroida, he explained in his own sweet time, is the queen-scorp of them idiotic scorpions that lives on Jupiter.

units.claim: Pard Hoskins previously sold the Halcyon Diamond to Akroida.
units.evidence: I sold her the Halcyon Diamond that disappeared from the World Museum five years ago

units.claim: The narrator felt envious and regretful about missing the opportunity to learn more about the emeralds.
units.evidence: Casey Ritter lost his nerve, and along with it, the chance of a lifetime.

units.claim: Pard Hoskins was part of a failed escape attempt and was locked up in the blockhouse.
units.evidence: Pard Hoskins was in the bunch. He'd never get out of there, and he knew it.

units.claim: Pard Hoskins was part of a group that attempted an escape but failed.
units.evidence: a group of lifers made a break that didn't jell, and the whole bunch was locked up in the blockhouse, the special building reserved for escapees. Pard Hoskins was in the bunch.

units.claim: Pard Hoskins believed he would not be able to leave the blockhouse.
units.evidence: He'd never get out of there, and he knew it.

units.claim: The narrator worked on his knuckles for three days after Pard's capture.
units.evidence: For three more days I worked down my knuckles, my nails being gone, while I sat around all hunched up, wondering feverishly if Pard would make a deal about those emeralds.

units.claim: The narrator sent a letter to the S.S.C.
units.evidence: Then I broke down and sent out a letter to the S.S.C.

units.claim: The Big Sneer visited the narrator and they discussed the caper.
units.evidence: The Big Sneer of the conference table promptly dropped in on me, friendly as a bottle of strychnine. But for a lad headed for Jupiter that was good training, so I sneered right back at him, explained the caper, and we both paid a visit to Pard.

units.claim: Pard Hoskins wore a yellow slicker to protect his spacesuit.
units.evidence: I put on a yeller slicker, that there ammonia mist was eatin' into the finish on my spacesuit, so I draped this here slicker around me to sorta fancy up the rig before goin' in to an audience with the old rip.

units.claim: Yellow drives the scorpions on Jupiter insane.
units.evidence: The kid that took me in was colorblind, so I didn't have no warning at all. I found out that them scorpions can't stand yeller. It just plain drives them nuts!

units.claim: Pard Hoskins created a perfume that drives the scorpions ecstatic.
units.evidence: Then I got off in a corner and cooked up some perfume that drives them nuts the other way; sorta frantic with ecstasy, like the book says.

units.claim: The perfume is stored in a purple bottle with a bright green stopper.
units.evidence: It's in the stuff they cleaned outa me room: a poiple bottle with a bright green stopper.

units.claim: Pard Hoskins suggested using a green and purple spacesuit with a touch of perfume to attract Akroida.
units.evidence: Make them shell out with a green an' poiple spacesuit—them's the real Jupiter colors—an' put just a touch o' that there perfume on the outside of it. Akroida'll do anything fer you if she just gets a whiff.

units.claim: The narrator was set to drift in the frozen ammonia clouds of Jupiter.
units.evidence: The day I was set adrift in that sea of frozen ammonia clouds mixed with nice cozy methane gas I sure prayed for it to be powerful, and I clutched that tiny bottle like that boy Aladdin clutching his little old lamp.

units.claim: Earth patrol retrieved the Killicut Emeralds from Mars.
units.evidence: An Earth patrol had slipped down onto the Red Desert of Mars and picked up the Killicut Emeralds from where Pard Hoskins had cached them;

units.claim: The narrator was to trade the emeralds for a secret.
units.evidence: These jewels are as nothing, Ritter, compared with the value of the secret you are to buy with them.

units.claim: If successful, the narrator would receive triple the market value of the emeralds and freedom.
units.evidence: if you succeed, your reward will be triple what you could get for them in any market. Added to which, IF you succeed, you will be a free man.

units.claim: The narrator was nervous and prepared for the journey to Jupiter.
units.evidence: I patted my pretty enameled suit, which was a study in paris green and passionate purple. I patted the three hundred pounds of arsenic crystals for Akroida and anyone else I might have to bribe. I anxiously examined my suit's air and water containers and the heating unit that would keep them in their proper state.

units.claim: The narrator entered Jupiter's atmosphere and encountered large red plants.
units.evidence: Surprise! The stuff was plants! Plants as big as meadows, bright red, floating around in those clouds of frozen ammonia like seaweed!

units.claim: The narrator saw a purple and green hopper-scorp approaching.
units.evidence: But my green boat must have showed up like a lighthouse in all that red, because it wasn't long until I spotted a purple and green hopper-scorp traveling straight toward me, sort of rowing along with a pair of stubby wings.

units.claim: They had covered two hundred miles before seeing something emerge from the mist.
units.evidence: It wasn't until we had covered some two hundred miles of this that something began to loom out of the mist

units.claim: The structure was red and made of compressed blocks of red plant.
units.evidence: It was red, like everything else in this screwy place, and could only have been built out of compressed blocks of the red plant.

units.claim: The structure was a perfect octagon.
units.evidence: In shape it was a perfect octagon.

units.claim: The structure was suspended in the center of a large clearing.
units.evidence: It hung poised in the center of the cleared space, suspended on nothing.

units.claim: The structure was at least a mile in diameter.
units.evidence: It had to be at least a mile in diameter

units.claim: The structure had thousands of openings through which its occupants appeared and disappeared.
units.evidence: Its sides were pierced with thousands of openings through which its nightmare occupants appeared and disappeared

units.claim: The narrator was led towards a window by Attaboy.
units.evidence: Attaboy was leading me straight across to a window.

units.claim: The narrator was carrying a hundred pounds of arsenic.
units.evidence: Picking up the first hundred pounds of the arsenic

units.claim: The building was floating two hundred miles from the edge of space.
units.evidence: it was floating up there only two hundred miles in from the raw edge of space.

units.claim: Objects in the building stayed where they were placed despite gravity.
units.evidence: If it was put twelve or fifty feet up off the floor, it stayed there.

units.claim: Attaboy carried the narrator to the central hall of the palace.
units.evidence: We finally came to the central hall of the palace

units.claim: The central hall was large enough to swallow a city block.
units.evidence: It was like a mammoth red cavern, and it glowed like the inside of a red light.

units.claim: Akroida was reclining on a green divan in the central hall.
units.evidence: A patch in the middle of the hall became a floating platform holding up a divan twenty feet square covered with stuff as green as new spring grass, and in the center of this reclined Akroida.

units.claim: Akroida was a violent purple color.
units.evidence: Our little Akroida was a pure and peculiarly violent purple—not a green edge anywhere.

units.claim: Akroida was wearing the Halcyon Diamond on her chest.
units.evidence: making the Halcyon Diamond on her chest blaze like a bonfire.

units.claim: Attaboy delivered a box to Akroida.
units.evidence: He closed in to the couch all hunched over, ducked his head humbly half-a-dozen times, and pushed the box over beside her.

units.claim: Akroida asked Attaboy who the box was from.
units.evidence: "Who from?" asked Akroida.

units.claim: Attaboy admitted the box was from an interspace trader named Casey Ritter.
units.evidence: "Dear lady, it is from an interspace trader who possesses some truly remarkable jewels," he confessed coyly.

units.claim: Akroida did not recognize Casey Ritter.
units.evidence: Casey Ritter? Never heard of him.

units.claim: Attaboy mentioned that the trader resembled an Earthman.
units.evidence: He does seem to resemble an—ah—earthman.

units.claim: Akroida reacted violently upon hearing the trader resembled an Earthman.
units.evidence: That old dame let out a scream like a maddened stallion and began to thrash around and flail her couch with that dragon's tail of hers.

units.claim: The narrator's green boat stood out in the red environment.
units.evidence: But my green boat must have showed up like a lighthouse in all that red

units.claim: A purple and green hopper-scorp was traveling towards the narrator.
units.evidence: I spotted a purple and green hopper-scorp traveling straight toward me

units.claim: The hopper-scorp was using a pair of stubby wings to move.
units.evidence: sort of rowing along with a pair of stubby wings

units.claim: The hopper-scorp did not seem to be making much effort to climb vertically.
units.evidence: He didn't seem to be making much effort, even though he was climbing vertically up from the planet

units.claim: Herrnstein and Murray estimate the heritability of IQ to be between 40% and 80%, with a middling estimate of 60%.
units.evidence: Herrnstein and Murray, sounding like the souls of caution, write that 'half a century of work, now amounting to hundreds of empirical and theoretical studies, permits a broad conclusion that the genetic component of IQ is unlikely to be smaller than 40 per cent or higher than 80 per cent. ... For purposes of this discussion, we will adopt a middling estimate of 60 per cent heritability.'

units.claim: Carnegie Mellon researchers found a lower heritability of IQ compared to Herrnstein and Murray's estimates.
units.evidence: Michael Daniels, Bernie Devlin, and Kathryn Roeder of Carnegie Mellon University took the same studies on which Herrnstein and Murray based their estimate, and subjected them to a computer meta-analysis ('a powerful method of statistical analysis'-- The Bell Curve ). Their paper, which has not yet been published, says: 'In brief, studies of IQ, and our reanalyses of them, suggest a narrow-sense heritability of 34 per cent and a broad-sense heritability of 46 per cent. [The difference between broad and narrow is too technical to explain in this limited space.] This is a far cry from Herrnstein and Murray's maximum value of 80 per cent or their middling value of 60 per cent. Consequently, Herrnstein and Murray give the impression that IQ is highly 'heritable,' but it is not.'

units.claim: The Bell Curve focuses on whether early-childhood programs like Head Start can raise IQ significantly over the long term.
units.evidence: The chapter of The Bell Curve on policies that might be able to overcome the fate of a low IQ focuses mainly on whether early-childhood programs like Head Start (most of which aren't run with raising IQ as their primary goal) can raise IQ significantly over the long term, and sorrowfully concludes that they can't.

You carefully poke the end of the hose into the ball of water, letting only the metal tip touch. Never the hose. If you let the hose touch, the water runs up it and tries to drown you. Then you pull up on the piston, and draw all the water into the cylinder.

units.evidence: Bale is such an expressive performer that Stuart's remembrance of things past attains a Proustian intensity.

units.claim: The scene where Arthur Stuart opens the new Brian Slade album is described as a vivid distillation of rock's allure.
units.evidence: To him, Slade was a sexual messiah. I've never seen a more vivid distillation of rock's allure than the scene in which he reverently opens the new Brian Slade album--its centerfold image is a lithe, naked, green-tinged Maxwell Demon--slips the vinyl out of its paper jacket and, after gingerly setting the LP on the turntable, props a chair under the doorknob to keep the uncomprehending world at bay.

units.claim: Haynes portrays Brian Slade as both an advocate for artifice and bisexuality and a hollow opportunist.
units.evidence: But if Haynes wants Velvet Goldmine to be an anthem to the principles Bowie once embodied--the embrace of artifice and the smashing of conventional sexual roles--he also wants to portray the rocker as a hollow opportunist who abandoned glam and bisexuality for the life of a corporate superstar, throwing in his lot with the forces of repression.

units.claim: Rhys-Meyers' portrayal of Brian Slade does not convey genuine thought or emotion.
units.evidence: An actor of stature might have bridged these two impulses, but the beautiful, brazenly slim-hipped Rhys-Meyers doesn't make his lines sound as if he's thinking them up on the spot, and Slade's self-destructive passion for Curt Wild (Ewan McGregor), the film's fuzzy, sweet Iggy Pop figure, seems less an emotional imperative than a thematic one.

units.claim: Velvet Goldmine may seem like a collection of signifiers without full substance.
units.evidence: A case can be made that Velvet Goldmine isn't fully filled in, and that Haynes, who has never shaken off his background as a semiotics major, has made a movie that's all signifiers.

units.claim: Claire Forlani plays the younger daughter in Meet Joe Black.
units.evidence: As the younger daughter, the dark eyed, spaghetti thin Claire Forlani has to carry the picture's bathos on her exquisite shoulders.
