units.claim: The narrator admits to being confused.
units.evidence: I admit it: I didn't know if I was coming or going—but I know that if I stuck to the old man, I was a comer ... even if he was a goner!

units.claim: Doc is holding a man by the throat.
units.evidence: Doc had this solemn human by the throat when I caught up with him.

units.claim: Doc believes tonight is the night humans will reach the Moon.
units.evidence: "Tonight," Doc was saying in his old voice that was as crackled and important as parchment, "tonight Man will reach the Moon."

units.claim: The man agrees with Doc but wants to be released.
units.evidence: "Sure," the man agreed severely, prying a little worriedly at Doc's arthritic fingers that were clamped on his collar.

units.claim: The narrator helps release Doc's grip on the man.
units.evidence: I came alongside and carefully started to lever the old man loose, one finger at a time.

units.claim: Doc's hands are described as old and crippled but very strong.
units.evidence: His hands looked old and crippled, but I felt they were the strongest in the world.

units.claim: The narrator has learned to handle Doc's behavior over weeks and months.
units.evidence: It had to be done this way. I had learned that during all these weeks and months.

units.claim: Doc's body is starting to shake, indicating an episode is coming on.
units.evidence: Doc's thin frame, layered with lumpy fat, was beginning to muscle-dance against my side. One of his times was coming on him.

units.claim: The narrator lies to the man about Doc's age and condition.
units.evidence: 'I hope you'll forgive him, sir,' I said, not meeting the man's eyes. 'He's my father and very old, as you can see.' I laughed inside at the absurd, easy lie. 'Old events seem recent to him.'

units.claim: The man offers to help but the narrator declines.
units.evidence: Say, the poor old guy looks sick. Want any help?' I told the human no, thanks, and walked Doc toward the flophouse three doors down.

units.claim: Martians are approaching the corner and sensing Doc and the narrator.
units.evidence: Martians approaching the corner were sensing at Doc and me.

units.claim: The narrator dislikes tourists, especially Martian tourists.
units.evidence: They were just cheap tourists slumming down on Skid Row. I hated tourists and especially I hated Martian tourists because I especially hated Martians.

units.claim: The narrator realizes he is about to experience an episode similar to Doc's.
units.evidence: Then I realized what was about to happen. It was foolish and awful and true. I was going to have one of mine at the same time Doc was having his.

units.claim: The narrator and Doc enter a flophouse.
units.evidence: I tried not to think about it and helped Doc through the fly-specked flophouse doors.

units.claim: The clerk charges fifteen cents per bed.
units.evidence: Fifteen cents a bed,

units.claim: The narrator offers twenty cents for one bed.
units.evidence: We'll use one bed, I told him. I'll give you twenty cents.

units.claim: The clerk accepts twenty cents for a room.
units.evidence: Awright, since we ain't full up. In advance.

units.claim: The narrator needs a nickel.
units.evidence: I knew I was going to need that nickel. Desperately.

units.claim: The narrator forces the clerk to give him a nickel.
units.evidence: I reached across the desk with my free hand and hauled the scrawny human up against the register hard.

units.claim: The room is small and poorly constructed.
units.evidence: The room was six feet in all directions and the walls were five feet high. The other foot was finished in chicken wire.

units.claim: There are other occupants in the room, including a wino singing and praying.
units.evidence: There was a wino singing on the left, a wino praying on the right, and the door didn't have any lock on it.

units.claim: The narrator lays Doc on a cot and shields his face from the light.
units.evidence: I laid Doc out on the gray-brown cot and put his forearm over his face to shield it some from the glare of the light bulb.

units.claim: The narrator removes visible bedbugs from the cot.
units.evidence: I swept off all the bedbugs in sight and stepped on them heavily.

units.claim: The narrator experiences a cramp and falls to the floor.
units.evidence: The cramp hit me and I folded out of the chair onto the littered, uncovered floor.

units.claim: Doc begins to mumble louder.
units.evidence: Doc began to mumble louder.

units.claim: The narrator knows he has to move despite the pain.
units.evidence: I knew I had to move.

units.claim: The narrator experienced a cramp that caused them to fall out of the chair.
units.evidence: The cramp hit me and I folded out of the chair onto the littered, uncovered floor.

units.claim: The narrator knew the cramp would return if they moved.
units.evidence: It stopped hurting, but I knew it would begin if I moved.

units.claim: Doc began to mumble louder.
units.evidence: Doc began to mumble louder.

units.claim: The narrator knew they had to move despite the pain.
units.evidence: I knew I had to move.

units.claim: The narrator managed to get from the floor to the chair and retrieve their notebook and orb-point.
units.evidence: I was bent double, but I got from the floor to the chair and found my notebook and orb-point in my hands.

units.claim: The narrator could not focus both their mind and eyes due to the pain.
units.evidence: I found I couldn't focus both my mind and my eyes through the electric flashes of agony, so I concentrated on Doc's voice and trusted my hands would follow their habit pattern and construct the symbols for his words.

units.claim: Doc's voice became a meaningless wail.
units.evidence: His voice rose to a meaningless wail that stretched into non-existence.

units.claim: The narrator believed the words spoken by Doc were crucial for becoming the most powerful man in the Solar Federation.
units.evidence: But I knew. Somehow, inside me, I knew that these words were what I had been waiting for. They told everything I needed to know to become the most powerful man in the Solar Federation.

units.claim: The narrator remembered that Doc was someone very important whose name and work they had once known.
units.evidence: When I got to thinking it was just a dream and that I was dragging this old man around North America for nothing, I remembered who he was. I remembered that he was somebody very important whose name and work I had once known, even if now I knew him only as Doc.

units.claim: The narrator experienced pain that varied in intensity.
units.evidence: Pain was a pendulum within me, swinging from low throbbing bass to high screaming tenor.

units.claim: The narrator needed to obtain something, possibly drugs, but did not have money.
units.evidence: I had to get out and get some. But I didn't have a nickel. Still, I had to get some.

units.claim: The narrator left Doc alone despite knowing they shouldn't.
units.evidence: I shouldn't leave Doc alone, but I had to.

units.claim: Doc started crying, which he did not always do.
units.evidence: He was starting to cry. He didn't always do that.

units.claim: The narrator comforted Doc by holding him and soothing his hair.
units.evidence: I shoved Doc's face up against my chest. I held onto him and let him bellow. I soothed the lanks of soiled white hair back over his lumpy skull.

units.claim: The narrator does not remember how they got out onto the street.
units.evidence: I don't remember how I got out onto the street.

units.claim: The woman the narrator approached at the bus stop was clean, pink, and wore a powder-blue dress.
units.evidence: She was pink and clean and her platinum hair was pulled straight back, drawing her cheek-bones tighter, straightening her wide, appealing mouth, drawing her lean, athletic, feminine body erect. She was wearing a powder-blue dress that covered all of her breasts and hips and the upper half of her legs.

units.claim: The narrator asked the woman for a dime for a cup of coffee.
units.evidence: Ma'am, could you help a man who's not had work? I kept my eyes down. I couldn't look a human in the eye and ask for help. Just a dime for a cup of coffee.

units.claim: The woman offered to buy the narrator dinner if she could go with him and ensure he ate it.
units.evidence: I'll buy you a dinner, she said carefully, provided I can go with you and see for myself that you actually eat it.

units.claim: The narrator felt bitter about accepting the woman's offer.
units.evidence: It was certainly unfair and probably immoral. But I had no choice whatever. Okay, I said, tasting bitterness over the craving.

units.claim: The narrator was a caffeine addict.
units.evidence: I was a caffeine addict.

units.claim: Caffeine affected the narrator's metabolism deeply.
units.evidence: Earth-norm humans sometimes have the addiction to a slight extent, but I knew that as a Centurian I had it infinitely worse. Caffeine affected my metabolism like a pure alkaloid.

units.claim: The narrator finished the cup of coffee without ordering another.
units.evidence: I finished the cup. I didn't order another because I wasn't a pure sensualist. I just needed release.

units.claim: The woman asked the narrator what they wanted to eat after drinking coffee.
units.evidence: Now what do you want to eat? the woman asked.

units.claim: Centurians have a deeper need for caffeine compared to Earth-norm humans.
units.evidence: Caffeine affected my metabolism like a pure alkaloid. The immediate effects weren't the same, but the need ran as deep.

units.claim: The narrator finishes a cup of coffee.
units.evidence: I finished the cup.

units.claim: The narrator does not order another cup of coffee because he is not a pure sensualist.
units.evidence: I didn't order another because I wasn't a pure sensualist.

units.claim: The narrator sometimes looks for leftover cola bottles in alleys for caffeine.
units.evidence: Sometimes, when I didn't have the price of a cup, I would look around in alleys and find cola bottles with a few drops left in them.

units.claim: The narrator is a Centurian who can pass as an Earth human.
units.evidence: Earthmen ran the whole Solar Federation, but I was just as good as an Earthman. With my suntan and short mane, I could pass, couldn't I?

units.claim: The narrator orders a well-done hamburger.
units.evidence: 'Hamburger,' I said. 'Well done.'

units.claim: The narrator is aware of his dirtiness and believes he cannot get clean.
units.evidence: I was so dirty, so very dirty that I could never get clean if I bathed every hour for the rest of my life.

units.claim: The narrator eats several hamburgers and drinks a glass of milk.
units.evidence: Several other hamburgers followed the first. I lost count. I drank a glass of milk.

units.claim: The narrator asks for hamburgers to take with him.
units.evidence: 'Could I have a few to take with me, miss?' I pleaded.

units.claim: Miss Casey introduces herself as Vivian Casey.
units.evidence: 'It's Miss Casey—Vivian Casey,' she corrected.

units.claim: The narrator gives his name as John Kevin.
units.evidence: 'Kevin,' I told her. 'John Kevin.'

units.claim: Miss Casey shows the narrator a coupon for 'The Scarlet Book'.
units.evidence: She pushed a white rectangle in front of me on the painted maroon bar. 'What do you think of this?'

units.claim: The narrator pays for his meal with a five dollar bill.
units.evidence: I looked up at his stubbled face. 'I had half a dozen hamburgers, a cup of coffee and a glass of milk. I want four more 'burgers to go and a pint of coffee. By your prices, that will be one sixty-five—if the lady didn't pay you.'

units.claim: The narrator leaves the diner and finds himself in a room with winos.
units.evidence: First I opened the door on an amber world, then an azure one. Neon light was coming from the chickenwire border of the room, from a window somewhere beyond. The wino on one side of the room was singing and the one on the other side was praying, same as before.

units.claim: Doc has created something using parts from a light bulb, bed springs, and an orb-point pen.
units.evidence: His strong hands had unraveled some of the bed 'springs'—metal webbing—and fashioned them to his needs. My orb-point pen had dissolved under his touch. All of them, useless parts, were made into a meaningful whole.

units.claim: Doc whispers 'An order, my boy, an order' to the narrator.
units.evidence: 'An order, my boy, an order,' he whispered.

units.claim: Doc writes 'First Edition' in the narrator's notebook.
units.evidence: The words 'First Edition' were what I was thinking about most.

units.claim: The narrator realizes that Doc's creation is related to time travel.
units.evidence: Then I realized what I had been trying to get from Doc all these months—time travel.

units.claim: Doc said 'Concentrate' hoarsely.
units.evidence: "Concentrate," Doc said hoarsely.

units.claim: The narrator was wondering about the meaning of the word 'concentrate'.
units.evidence: I wondered what the words meant.

units.claim: Wondering requires a form of concentration.
units.evidence: Wondering takes a kind of concentration.

units.claim: The narrator was thinking about the words 'First Edition'.
units.evidence: The words 'First Edition' were what I was thinking about most.

units.claim: A heavy-set man in an ornate armchair mentioned being struck by a bullet while pulling on his boot.
units.evidence: The heavy-set man in the ornate armchair was saying, 'The bullet struck me as I was pulling on my boot....'

units.claim: The narrator was kneeling on the floor of a Victorian living room.
units.evidence: I was kneeling on the floor of a Victorian living room.

units.claim: The narrator recognized the period as Victorian due to familiarity with Earth history.
units.evidence: I'm quite familiar with Earth history and I recognized the period immediately.

units.claim: The narrator realized that Doc had been trying to convey the concept of time travel.
units.evidence: Then I realized what I had been trying to get from Doc all these months—time travel.

units.claim: A thin, sickly man was sprawled in a rumpled dressing gown.
units.evidence: A thin, sickly man was sprawled in the other chair in a rumpled dressing gown.

units.claim: The thin man had pinpoint pupils and a whitened nose.
units.evidence: My eyes held to his face, his pinpoint pupils and whitened nose.

units.claim: The thin man was referred to as a 'snowbird'.
units.evidence: He was a condemned snowbird!

units.claim: The thin man commented on the unusual methods of entry into the room.
units.evidence: My clients have occasioned singular methods of entry into these rooms, but never before have they used instantaneous materialization.

units.claim: The heavier man was half choking and half laughing.
units.evidence: The heavier man was half choking, half laughing.

units.claim: The thin man stated he had no data regarding the narrator's arrival.
units.evidence: 'I have no data,' the thin man answered coolly.

units.claim: The thin man suggested twisting theories into fact or vice versa.
units.evidence: In such instance, one begins to twist theories into fact, or facts into theories.

units.claim: The thin man asked the narrator to provide the place and time from which he came.
units.evidence: I must ask this unemployed, former professional man who has gone through a serious illness and is suffering a more serious addiction to tell me the place and time from which he comes.

units.claim: The narrator was surprised by the thin man's knowledge.
units.evidence: The surprise stung. 'How did you know?' I asked.

units.claim: The thin man maintained a logical approach and rejected the supernatural.
units.evidence: To maintain a logical approach, I must reject the supernatural.

units.claim: The thin man considered the narrator's arrival as super-normal or super-scientific.
units.evidence: Your arrival was then super-normal. I might say super-scientific, of a science not of my or the good doctor's time, clearly.

units.claim: The thin man mentioned time travel as a familiar folk legend and referenced H.G. Wells.
units.evidence: Time travel is a familiar folk legend and I have been reading an article by the entertaining Mr. Wells.

units.claim: The narrator recognized the two men but with a doubt.
units.evidence: I knew who these two men were, with a tormenting doubt.

units.claim: The thin man observed the narrator's hands and judged him to have suffered an illness.
units.evidence: Your hands, though unclean, have never seen physical labor. Your cranial construction is of a superior type, or even if you reject my theories, concentration does set the facial features. I judge you have suffered an illness because of the inhibition of your beard growth.

units.claim: The thin man noted the narrator's over-fondness for rum or opium.
units.evidence: Your over-fondness for rum or opium, perhaps, is self-evident.

units.claim: The narrator hated the thin man because he couldn't trust his own senses as the thin man could.
units.evidence: Because I couldn't trust to my own senses as he did.

units.claim: The narrator claimed the two men were fictional creations.
units.evidence: 'You don't exist,' I said slowly, painfully. 'You are fictional creations.'

units.claim: The doctor flushed darkly in response to the narrator's statement.
units.evidence: The doctor flushed darkly.

units.claim: The thin man filled a large, curved pipe from something resembling an ice-skate.
units.evidence: The other man was filling a large, curved pipe from something that looked vaguely like an ice-skate.

units.claim: The thin man suggested the narrator provide information about his age and temporal transference.
units.evidence: 'Perhaps if our visitor would tell us something of his age with special reference to the theory and practice of temporal transference, Doctor, we would be better equipped to judge whether we exist.'

units.claim: The narrator explained all he had heard about time travel theories.
units.evidence: I told them all I had ever heard theorized from Hindu yoga through Extra-sensory Perception to Relativity and the positron and negatron.

units.claim: The thin man suggested that people of the narrator's time may have altered the past.
units.evidence: Presume that the people of your time by their 'Extra-sensory Perception' have altered the past to make it as they suppose it to be.

units.claim: The thin man mentioned the historical figures being larger than life-size.
units.evidence: The great historical figures are made the larger than life-size that we know them.

units.claim: The thin man noted his hand had indented a round brass weight.
units.evidence: His tapered fingertips had indented the metal.

units.claim: King Richard warned of a potential flank attack from the eastern hills.
units.evidence: The King turned to Sir Baldwin de Carreo, who sat ahorse nearby, and pointed toward the eastern hills. "They will come from there, hitting us in the flank; we cannot afford to amass a rearward charge. To do so would be to fall directly into the hands of the Saracen."

units.claim: Sir Gaeton agreed with King Richard's assessment.
units.evidence: A voice very close to Sir Robert said: "Richard is right. If we go to the aid of the Hospitallers, we will expose the column to a flank attack." It was Sir Gaeton.

units.claim: Sir Robert proposed a charge to break the Egyptian line.
units.evidence: "My lord the King," Sir Robert heard his voice say, "is right in all but one thing. If we allow the Egyptians to take us from the rear, there will be no need for Saladin and his Turks to come down on our flank. And the Hospitallers cannot hold for long at this rate. A charge at full gallop would break the Egyptian line and give the Hospitallers breathing time. Are you with me?"

units.claim: Sir Gaeton agreed to join Sir Robert's charge.
units.evidence: After a moment's hesitation, Sir Gaeton couched his lance. "I'm with you, sir knight! Live or die, I follow! Strike and strike hard!"

units.claim: Sir Robert and Sir Gaeton charged towards the battle lines.
units.evidence: Two great war horses began to move ponderously forward toward the battle lines, gaining momentum as they went. Moving in unison, the two knights, their horses now at a fast trot, lowered their lances, picking their Saracen targets with care.

units.claim: Sir Robert's lance struck a Saracen horseman in the chest.
units.evidence: Sir Robert felt the shock against himself and his horse as the steel tip of the long ash lance struck the Saracen horseman in the chest.

units.claim: Sir Robert's lance was impeded by the Saracen's lighter armor.
units.evidence: His lighter armor had hardly impeded the incoming spear-point, and now his body dragged it down as he dropped toward the desert sand.

units.claim: Sir Robert dropped his lance and drew his broadsword.
units.evidence: There was nothing else to do but drop the lance and draw his heavy broadsword. His hand grasped it, and it came singing from its scabbard.

units.claim: Sir Robert's broadsword decapitated an Egyptian cavalryman.
units.evidence: In return, the knight's broadsword came about in a sweeping arc, and the Egyptian's horse rode on with the rider's headless body.

units.claim: Hospitallers rallied and joined the charge.
units.evidence: The Hospitallers, taking heart at the charge, were going in! Behind them came the Count of Champagne, the Earl of Leister, and the Bishop of Beauvais, who carried a great warhammer in order that he might not break Church Law by shedding blood.

units.claim: Sir Robert felt detached during the battle.
units.evidence: He himself felt a dreamlike detachment, as though he were watching the battle rather than participating in it.

units.claim: Moslems were falling back before the Christian onslaught.
units.evidence: But he could see that the Moslems were falling back before the Christian onslaught.

units.claim: Sir Robert and Sir Gaeton sheathed their swords after the battle.
units.evidence: Breathing heavily, Sir Robert sheathed his broadsword.

units.claim: Sir Gaeton believed they may have routed the enemy.
units.evidence: Sir Gaeton did the same, saying: "It will be a few minutes before they can regroup, sir knight. We may have routed them completely."

units.claim: Sir Robert worried about disobeying King Richard's orders.
units.evidence: "Aye. But King Richard will not approve of my breaking ranks and disobeying orders. I may win the battle and lose my head in the end."

units.claim: Sir Gaeton suggested resting after the battle.
units.evidence: "This is no time to worry about the future," said the Gascon. "Rest for a moment and relax, that you may be the stronger later. Here—have an Old Kings."

units.claim: Sir Gaeton offered Sir Robert a cigarette.
units.evidence: He had a pack of cigarettes in his gauntleted hand, which he profferred to Sir Robert.

units.claim: Sir Robert accepted a cigarette from Sir Gaeton.
units.evidence: Sir Robert's hand reached out and took that one.

units.claim: Sir Robert enjoyed smoking an Old Kings cigarette.
units.evidence: "Thanks. When the going gets rough, I really enjoy an Old Kings."

units.claim: Sir Gaeton lit his own cigarette.
units.evidence: He put one end of the cigarette in his mouth and lit the other from the lighter in Sir Gaeton's hand.

units.claim: Sir Gaeton praised Old Kings cigarettes.
units.evidence: "Yes, sir," said Sir Gaeton, after lighting his own cigarette, "Old Kings are the greatest. They give a man real, deep-down smoking pleasure."

units.claim: Sir Robert felt the soothing effect of smoking an Old Kings cigarette.
units.evidence: Sir Robert could feel the soothing smoke in his lungs as he inhaled deeply.

units.claim: Sir Gaeton agreed that Old Kings is the only real cigarette for real men's work.
units.evidence: "Nor I," agreed the Gascon. "Old Kings is the only real cigarette when you're doing a real man's work."

units.claim: Sir Gaeton believes Old Kings are the greatest cigarettes.
units.evidence: Old Kings are the greatest. They give a man real, deep-down smoking pleasure.

units.claim: Sir Robert agrees that Old Kings are a man's cigarette.
units.evidence: There's no doubt about it, Old Kings are a man's cigarette.

units.claim: Sir Robert inhales deeply and feels the soothing smoke in his lungs.
units.evidence: Sir Robert could feel the soothing smoke in his lungs as he inhaled deeply.

units.claim: Sir Robert prefers Old Kings when he wants a cigarette.
units.evidence: When I want a cigarette, I don't want just any cigarette.

units.claim: The Gascon knight agrees that Old Kings is the only real cigarette for real man's work.
units.evidence: Old Kings is the only real cigarette when you're doing a real man's work.

units.claim: Sir Robert watches a smoke ring expand in the air.
units.evidence: That's for sure.

units.claim: There is a sudden clash of arms to their left.
units.evidence: There was a sudden clash of arms off to their left.

units.claim: Sir Robert drops his cigarette to the ground.
units.evidence: Sir Robert dropped his cigarette to the ground.

units.claim: Sir Robert acknowledges that doing real he-man's work does not always allow enjoying Old Kings right to the end.
units.evidence: The trouble is that doing a real he-man's work doesn't always allow you to enjoy the fine, rich tobaccos of Old Kings right down to the very end.

units.claim: The Gascon knight suggests lighting another Old Kings later.
units.evidence: No, but you can always light another later.

units.claim: King Richard charges through the Hospitallers to join the fray.
units.evidence: King Richard, on seeing his army moving suddenly toward the harassed rear, had realized the danger and had charged through the Hospitallers to get into the thick of the fray.

units.claim: Turks charge down from the hills, hitting the rear of the army.
units.evidence: Now the Turks were charging down from the hills, hitting—not the flank as he had expected, but the rear!

units.claim: Saladin expected King Richard to hold fast.
units.evidence: Saladin had expected him to hold fast!

units.claim: Sir Robert and Sir Gaeton spur their horses towards the English banner.
units.evidence: Sir Robert and Sir Gaeton spurred their chargers toward the flapping banner of England.

units.claim: King Richard cuts down Turks as if they were grain-stalks.
units.evidence: The fierce warrior-king of England, his mighty sword in hand, was cutting down Turks as though they were grain-stalks.

units.claim: Sir Robert keeps his great broadsword moving to hack down the Moslem foes.
units.evidence: There was nothing to do but keep his own great broadsword moving, swinging like some gigantic metronome as he hacked down the Moslem foes.

units.claim: Sir Robert finds himself surrounded by Saracens and isolated from the rest of the Christian forces.
units.evidence: He was isolated and alone, cut off from the rest of the Christian forces!

units.claim: Sir Robert sees the red-and-gold banner of Richard far to the rear.
units.evidence: He caught a glimpse of the fluttering banner far to the rear and started to fall back.

units.claim: Sir Robert sees King Richard nearby, wearing a golden coronet on his steel helm.
units.evidence: On his steel helm gleamed a golden coronet! Richard!

units.claim: King Richard is heavily outnumbered and will soon be cut down by the Saracen horde.
units.evidence: In spite of his prowess was outnumbered heavily and would, within seconds, be cut down by the Saracen horde!

units.claim: Sir Robert plunges his horse towards the surrounded monarch to save him.
units.evidence: Without hesitation, Sir Robert plunged his horse toward the surrounded monarch, his great blade cutting a path before him.

units.claim: Sir Robert fights to protect the fallen King Richard.
units.evidence: hearing the familiar cry of 'For St. George and for England' behind him.

units.claim: Richard gets back on his feet and starts fighting again.
units.evidence: And then Richard was on his feet, cleaving the air about him with his own broadsword.

units.claim: The Turks begin to fall back and retreat.
units.evidence: The Turks began to fall back. Within seconds, the Christian knights were boiling around the embattled pair, forcing the Turks into retreat.

units.claim: King Richard thanks Sir Robert for his service.
units.evidence: You have done well this day, sir knight. Richard Plantagenet will not forget.

units.claim: Sir Robert pledges his loyalty to King Richard.
units.evidence: My lord king, be assured that I would never forget my loyalty to my sovereign and liege lord. My sword and my life are yours whenever you call.

units.claim: King Richard promises an earldom to Sir Robert upon returning to England.
units.evidence: An earldom awaits you when we return to England, sir knight.

units.claim: King Richard rides after the retreating Saracens.
units.evidence: And then the king mounted his horse and was running full gallop after the retreating Saracens.

units.claim: Robert takes off his helmet and adjusts his eyes to the dimness of the studio.
units.evidence: Robert took off his helmet. He blinked for a second to adjust his eyes to the relative dimness of the studio.

units.claim: Robert is asked how he liked the experience.
units.evidence: How'd you like it, Bob?

units.claim: Robert thinks the commercial is O.K. but needs improvements.
units.evidence: It was O.K.," he said. "Good show. A little talky at the beginning, and it needs a better fade-out, but the action scenes were fine.

units.claim: Robert believes the sponsor will lose sales if the commercial airs as is.
units.evidence: If this thing goes on the air the way it is, he'll lose sales.

units.claim: Robert thinks the commercial's cigarette tastes better than the real Old Kings.
units.evidence: Too good! Man, I've smoked Old Kings, and, believe me, the real thing never tasted as good as that cigarette did in the commercial!

units.claim: The source is a work of fiction titled 'DISTURBING SUN' by Philip Latham.
units.evidence: DISTURBING SUN By PHILIP LATHAM

units.evidence: Illustrated by Freas

units.claim: Dr. I. M. Niemand is the Director of the Psychophysical Institute of Solar and Terrestrial Relations in Camarillo, California.
units.evidence: An interview with Dr. I. M. Niemand, Director of the Psychophysical Institute of Solar and Terrestrial Relations, Camarillo, California.

units.claim: Dr. Niemand delivered a paper entitled 'On the Nature of the Solar S-Regions' at the American Association for the Advancement of Science meeting in New York in December 1957.
units.evidence: In the closing days of December, 1957, at the meeting of the American Association for the Advancement of Science in New York, Dr. Niemand delivered a paper entitled simply, 'On the Nature of the Solar S-Regions.'

units.claim: Sunspots are regions on the Sun that are cooler than their surroundings.
units.evidence: A sunspot is a region on the Sun that is cooler than its surroundings.

units.claim: The number of sunspots rises and falls in a cycle of about eleven years.
units.evidence: The number of spots on the Sun rises and falls in a cycle of about eleven years.

units.claim: There is a correlation between sunspots and disturbances of the Earth's magnetic field, radio fade-outs, and auroras.
units.evidence: There is unquestionably a correlation between sunspots and disturbances of the Earth's magnetic field ... radio fade-outs ... auroras ... things like that.

units.claim: S-Regions are invisible to the eye but can be detected by suitable instruments.
units.evidence: It is quite invisible to the eye but readily detected by suitable instrumental methods.

units.claim: S-Regions are named after the Sun.
units.evidence: Named after the Sun, I suppose.

units.claim: Dr. Niemand believes that S-Regions, not sunspots, are the cause of disturbances on Earth.
units.evidence: I think our biggest advance was the discovery that sunspots themselves are not the direct cause of the disturbances we have been studying on the Earth.

units.claim: Historical records show periods of calm followed by sudden reversals into chaos and war.
units.evidence: Consider the record of history. There are occasional periods when conditions are fairly calm and peaceful. Art and industry flourished. Man at last seemed to be making progress toward some higher goal. Then suddenly—for no detectable reason—conditions are reversed. Wars rage. People go mad. The world is plunged into an orgy of bloodshed and misery.

units.claim: Dr. Niemand suggests that forces outside of humans, possibly related to the Sun, may be responsible for human evil and conflict.
units.evidence: Men go to war because they want to go to war. They can't help themselves. They are impelled by forces over which they have no control. By forces outside of themselves.

units.claim: An attack is considered simultaneous if it occurs within five minutes of an attack on the opposite coast.
units.evidence: We say an attack is simultaneous when one occurred on the east coast, for example, not earlier or later than five minutes of an attack on the west coast.

units.claim: In every case of a simultaneous attack, the Sun was shining in both New York and California.
units.evidence: In every case of a simultaneous attack the Sun was shining at both New York and California.

units.claim: The Sun had to be above the horizon at both places for an attack to occur.
units.evidence: I mean the Sun had to be above the horizon at both places.

units.claim: Attacks occurred only during daylight hours.
units.evidence: We had both noticed that the attacks occurred only during the daylight hours

units.claim: Dr. Hillyard and Niemand had been searching for a clue regarding the attacks.
units.evidence: Dr. Hillyard and I had been searching desperately for a clue.

units.claim: Hillyard knew Henry Middletown, an astrophysicist, who helped with the investigation.
units.evidence: Several years before Hillyard had gotten to know a young astrophysicist, Henry Middletown, who had come to him suffering from a severe case of myositis in the arms and shoulders.

units.claim: Middletown specialized in radio astronomy at the government's new solar observatory on Turtle Back Mountain in Arizona.
units.evidence: Middletown was now specializing in radio astronomy at the government's new solar observatory on Turtle Back Mountain in Arizona.

units.claim: Without Middletown's help, the investigation would not have progressed beyond the clinical stage.
units.evidence: If it had not been for Middletown's help I'm afraid our investigation would never have gotten past the clinical stage.

units.claim: Middletown created a chart showing the number and intensity of attacks over time.
units.evidence: First, he laid out a series of about thirty squares horizontally across a sheet of graph paper. He dated these beginning March 1, 1955, when our records began. In each square he put a number from 1 to 10 that was a rough index of the number and intensity of the attacks reported on that day.

units.claim: The chart showed that the days of highest index number fell in slightly slanting parallel series.
units.evidence: When Middletown had finished it was easy to see that the squares of highest index number did not fall at random on the chart. Instead they fell in slightly slanting parallel series so that you could draw straight lines down through them.

units.claim: The synodic period of solar rotation is approximately twenty-seven days.
units.evidence: twenty-seven days is about the synodic period of solar rotation.

units.claim: On the second chart, the squares were dated under one another at intervals of twenty-seven point three days.
units.evidence: On this second chart the squares were dated under one another not at intervals of twenty-seven days, but at intervals of twenty-seven point three days.

units.claim: The average period of solar rotation in the sunspot zone is twenty-seven point three days.
units.evidence: Because the average period of solar rotation in the sunspot zone is not twenty-seven days but twenty-seven point three days.

units.claim: There was a lag of about forty-eight hours between the disturbances on the Earth and those due to the S-Regions on the Sun.
units.evidence: The disturbances on the Earth started two days later on the average than the disturbances due to the S-Regions on the Sun. In other words, there was a lag of about forty-eight hours between the two.

units.claim: S-Regions are invisible to the eye through an optical telescope but are detected with ease by a radio telescope.
units.evidence: The S-Regions are invisible to the eye through an optical telescope, but are detected with ease by a radio telescope.

units.claim: Middletown discovered S-Regions while working on radio astronomy in Australia.
units.evidence: Middletown had discovered them when he was a graduate student working on radio astronomy in Australia.

units.claim: The formation of an S-Region is heralded by a long series of bursts of a few seconds duration.
units.evidence: The formation of an S-Region is heralded by a long series of bursts of a few seconds duration, when the radiation may increase up to several thousand times that of the background intensity.

units.claim: Noise storms have been recorded simultaneously on wavelengths of from one to fifteen meters.
units.evidence: These noise storms have been recorded simultaneously on wavelengths of from one to fifteen meters, which so far is the upper limit of the observations.

units.claim: Intense bursts have also been detected down to fifty cm.
units.evidence: In a few instances, however, intense bursts have also been detected down to fifty cm.

units.claim: Latham asks if there were reasons for something.
units.evidence: But weren't there reasons?

units.claim: Niemand questions what reasons Latham is referring to.
units.evidence: What reasons?

units.claim: Latham suggests disputes over boundaries, economic rivalry, and border incidents as potential reasons.
units.evidence: Well, disputes over boundaries ... economic rivalry ... border incidents....

units.claim: Niemand dismisses the suggested reasons as nonsense.
units.evidence: Nonsense.

units.claim: Niemand believes men go to war because they want to and are driven by uncontrollable forces.
units.evidence: Men always make some flimsy excuse for going to war. The truth of the matter is that men go to war because they want to go to war. They can't help themselves. They are impelled by forces over which they have no control. By forces outside of themselves.

units.claim: Latham requests Niemand to be more specific.
units.evidence: Those are broad, sweeping statements. Can't you be more specific?

units.claim: Niemand starts recounting events from March 1955.
units.evidence: Perhaps I'd better go back to the beginning. Let me see.... It all started back in March, 1955,...

units.claim: In March 1955, Niemand started seeing patients with symptoms including profound mental depression, anxiety, insomnia, and fits of violent rage.
units.evidence: ... when I started getting patients suffering from a complex of symptoms, such as profound mental depression, anxiety, insomnia, alternating with fits of violent rage and resentment against life and the world in general.

units.claim: The patients were deeply disturbed but not psychotic or severely neurotic.
units.evidence: These people were deeply disturbed. No doubt about that. Yet they were not psychotic and hardly more than mildly neurotic.

units.claim: The patients came from various backgrounds and ages.
units.evidence: They were married and single persons of both sexes and of all ages. They came from all walks of life.

units.claim: The onset of the attacks was sudden and without warning.
units.evidence: The onset of their attack was invariably sudden and with scarcely any warning.

units.claim: The attacks ceased as mysteriously as they began.
units.evidence: A week or ten days later the attack would cease as mysteriously as it had come and they would be their old self again.

units.claim: Latham suggests that such attacks might be characteristic of the stress and strain of modern life.
units.evidence: Aren't such attacks characteristic of the stress and strain of modern life?

units.claim: Niemand believes the stress-and-strain theory has been overused.
units.evidence: I'm afraid that old stress-and-strain theory has been badly overworked.

units.claim: Niemand mentions that the stress-and-strain theory has been discussed since his pre-med studies at UCLA.
units.evidence: Even as a boy I can remember my grandfather deploring the stress and strain of modern life when he was a country doctor practicing in Indiana. In my opinion one of the most valuable contributions anthropologists have made in recent years is the discovery that primitive man is afflicted with essentially the same neurotic conditions as those of us who live a so-called civilized life.

units.claim: Anthropologists have found similar neurotic conditions in primitive societies.
units.evidence: They have found savages displaying every symptom of a nervous breakdown among the mountain tribes of the Elgonyi and the Aruntas of Australia.

units.claim: Niemand believes the stress-and-strain theory should be discarded.
units.evidence: No, Mr. Latham, it's time the stress-and-strain theory was relegated to the junk pile along with demoniac possession and blood letting.

units.claim: Latham asks if Niemand did anything for his patients.
units.evidence: You must have done something for your patients—

units.claim: Niemand explains that doctors must always do something for their patients.
units.evidence: A doctor must always do something for the patients who come to his office seeking help.

units.claim: Niemand provided his patients with a thorough physical examination.
units.evidence: First I gave them a thorough physical examination.

units.claim: Minor ailments were found in some patients, but nothing significant.
units.evidence: I turned up some minor ailments—a slight heart murmur or a trace of albumin in the urine—but nothing of any significance.

units.claim: The patients were generally healthy.
units.evidence: On the whole they were a remarkably healthy bunch of individuals, much more so than an average sample of the population.

units.claim: Niemand inquired into the personal lives of his patients.
units.evidence: Then I made a searching inquiry into their personal life.

units.claim: The personal inquiries did not reveal significant issues.
units.evidence: Here again I drew a blank. They had no particular financial worries. Their sex life was generally satisfactory. There was no history of mental illness in the family.

units.claim: The only issue was that the patients sometimes felt terrible.
units.evidence: In fact, the only thing that seemed to be the matter with them was that there were times when they felt like hell.

units.claim: Latham asks if Niemand tried tranquilizers.
units.evidence: I suppose you tried tranquilizers?

units.claim: Niemand tried tranquilizers in a few cases with slight improvement.
units.evidence: Oh, yes. In a few cases in which I tried tranquilizing pills of the meprobamate type there was some slight improvement.

units.claim: Niemand does not believe in prescribing shotgun remedies.
units.evidence: To my way of thinking it is a lazy slipshod way of carrying on the practice of medicine.

units.claim: Niemand asked his patients to keep a detailed record of their symptoms.
units.evidence: The only thing for which I do give myself credit was that I asked my patients to keep a detailed record of their symptoms taking special care to note the time of exacerbation—increase in the severity of the symptoms—as accurately as possible.

units.claim: Latham asks if the records gave Niemand a clue.
units.evidence: And this gave you a clue?

units.claim: The records were the beginning of finding a pattern.
units.evidence: It was the beginning.

units.claim: Patients reported attacks occurring suddenly with slight prodromal symptoms.
units.evidence: In most instances patients reported the attack struck with almost the impact of a physical blow. The prodromal symptoms were usually slight ... a sudden feeling of uneasiness and guilt ... hot and cold flashes ... dizziness ... double vision.

units.claim: The attacks included a sense of depression and rage.
units.evidence: Then this ghastly sense of depression coupled with a blind insensate rage at life.

units.claim: Some patients felt the world was closing in on them or that others were plotting their destruction.
units.evidence: One man said he felt as if the world were closing in on him. Another that he felt the people around him were plotting his destruction.

units.claim: One patient's husband locked her in her room out of fear she would injure the children.
units.evidence: One housewife made her husband lock her in her room for fear she would injure the children.

units.claim: Niemand analyzed the case histories but initially got nowhere.
units.evidence: I pored over these case histories for a long time getting absolutely nowhere.

units.claim: Eventually, a pattern began to emerge.
units.evidence: Then finally a pattern began to emerge.

units.claim: The attacks occurred during the daytime, between 7 AM and 5 PM.
units.evidence: The first thing that struck me was that the attacks all occurred during the daytime, between the hours of about seven in the morning and five in the evening.

units.claim: There were coincidences in the timing of the attacks.
units.evidence: Then there were these coincidences—

units.claim: Total strangers miles apart experienced attacks at almost the same moment.
units.evidence: Total strangers miles apart were stricken at almost the same moment.

units.claim: Mathematical analysis showed the coincidences followed a Poisson distribution.
units.evidence: A mathematical analysis showed the number of coincidences followed a Poisson distribution very closely.

units.claim: Niemand did not tell his patients about the coincidences.
units.evidence: Naturally I said nothing of this to my patients.

units.claim: Niemand emphasized the importance of accurate records to his patients.
units.evidence: I did, however, take pains to impress upon them the necessity of keeping an exact record of the onset of an attack.

units.claim: Better records led to more conclusive evidence.
units.evidence: The better records they kept the more conclusive was the evidence.

units.claim: Simultaneous attacks occurred across southern California.
units.evidence: Men and women were experiencing nearly simultaneous attacks of rage and depression all over southern California, which was as far as my practice extended.

units.claim: Niemand considered the possibility of simultaneous attacks occurring thousands of miles apart.
units.evidence: if people a few miles apart could be stricken simultaneously, why not people hundreds or thousands of miles apart?

units.claim: Niemand contacted Dr. Max Hillyard, an old colleague in Utica, New York.
units.evidence: It was this idea that prompted me to get in touch with an old colleague of mine I had known at UC medical school, Dr. Max Hillyard, who was in practice in Utica, New York.

units.claim: Niemand was surprised and gratified to find Dr. Hillyard had similar patients.
units.evidence: Imagine my surprise and gratification on receiving an answer by return mail to the effect that he also had been getting an increasing number of patients suffering with the same identical symptoms as my own.

units.claim: Upon exchanging records, Niemand and Dr. Hillyard found simultaneous attacks occurring thousands of miles apart.
units.evidence: Furthermore, upon exchanging records we did find that in many cases patients three thousand miles apart had been stricken simultaneously—

units.claim: Latham asks for clarification on the definition of 'simultaneous'.
units.evidence: Just a minute. I would like to know how you define 'simultaneous.'

units.claim: Niemand defines 'simultaneous' as within five minutes of each other.
units.evidence: We say an attack is simultaneous when one occurred on the east coast, for example, not earlier or later than five minutes of an attack on the west coast.

units.evidence: Noon mess was nearly as awful as breakfast had been.

units.claim: The coffee at noon tasted salty and was mostly undrunk.
units.evidence: The coffee tasted of salt, and went largely undrunk.

units.claim: The crew blamed the Captain for the poor quality of the food.
units.evidence: The men in the mess compartment were vehement in their protests, blaming the Captain, in his absence, for the decline in culinary standards.

units.claim: Bailey served the algaeburgers indifferently and ignored the crew's taunts.
units.evidence: Bailey seemed not to care. He served the algaeburgers with half a mind, and hurried back into his galley oblivious of the taunts of his crewmates.

units.claim: The mess compartment had only three seats, so meals were eaten in three shifts.
units.evidence: There being only three seats in the Sale's mess compartment, we ate our meals in three shifts.

units.claim: The evening meal smelled like barbecue, evoking pleasant outdoor dining memories.
units.evidence: my nose was met with a spine-tingling barbecue tang, a smell to make a man think of gray charcoal glowing in a picnic brazier, of cicadas chirping and green grass underfoot, of the pop and hiss of canned beer being church-keyed.

units.claim: The first-shift diner noted that the food actually tasted good.
units.evidence: "He's done it, Doc!" one of the first-shift diners said. "It actually tastes of food!"

units.claim: The narrator stated that the Captain would not want to criticize the improved food.
units.evidence: The Dutchman won't want to mess ketchup on these steaks

units.claim: The narrator observed that the steaks were drenched in a rich, peppery gravy.
units.evidence: Each contained about a pound of dried Chlorella, I judged, teasing mine with my fork. But they were drenched in a gravy rich as the stuff grandma used to make in her black iron skillet, peppery and seasoned with courageous bits of garlic.

units.claim: The narrator complimented Bailey on making the food taste good.
units.evidence: This is actually good.

units.claim: The narrator explained that the Captain's tough approach helped Bailey improve.
units.evidence: He drove you to this triumph; you couldn't have done it without him.

units.claim: Bailey asked if the narrator liked the Captain.
units.evidence: Do you like Captain Winkelmann, Doctor?

units.claim: The narrator admitted liking the Captain despite his methods.
units.evidence: Bailey, I'm afraid I'll have to admit that I do.

units.claim: Bailey offered the narrator an additional steak.
units.evidence: Bailey smiled and lifted a second steak from the warming-pan onto my plate. "Then have another piece," he said.

units.claim: Someone asks Bailey if he has been working on the problem of steak.
units.evidence: I've been working on the problem of steak, Sir,

units.claim: Bailey thinks he has improved the taste of the steak substitute.
units.evidence: I think I've whipped the taste;

units.claim: Bailey is working on making the texture of the steak substitute similar to real steak.
units.evidence: what was left was to get the texture steak-like.

units.claim: Bailey uses Chlorella with special seasonings to create the steak substitute.
units.evidence: I squeezed the steak-substrate—Chlorella, of course, with all sorts of special seasonings—

units.claim: Bailey processes the Chlorella through a sieve and blanches it in hot algaeal oil.
units.evidence: through a sieve, and blanched the strands in hot algaeal oil.

units.claim: Bailey chops and rolls out the processed Chlorella to achieve a texture similar to muscle fibers of genuine meat.
units.evidence: Then I chopped those strands to bits and rolled them out.

units.claim: The Captain expresses disgust at hearing the details of how the food is prepared.
units.evidence: It rather throws me off my appetite to hear how you muddle about with our food,

units.claim: The Captain prefers not to see the preparation process of the food.
units.evidence: but I never cared to see the ugly beast boiled before my eyes.

units.claim: Bailey serves the algaeal steak to the Captain and others.
units.evidence: Bailey lifted the cover off the electric warming-pan at the center of the table and tenderly lifted a small 'steak' onto each of our plates.

units.claim: The algaeal steak has a color similar to medium-rare meat and smells like fresh-broiled beef.
units.evidence: The color was an excellent medium-rare, the odor was the rich smell of fresh-broiled beef.

units.claim: The Captain finds the algaeal steak not too bad after tasting it.
units.evidence: Not too bad, Belly-Robber,

units.claim: The Captain believes the algaeal steak still needs improvement.
units.evidence: But it still needs something ... something,

units.claim: The Captain adds ketchup to the algaeal steak and considers it the perfect addition.
units.evidence: Winkelmann reached beneath the mess-table and ripped open his cardboard carton. He brought out a bottle and unscrewed the cap. 'Ketchup,' he said, splattering the red juice over Bailey's masterpiece. 'The scarlet burial-shroud for the failures of Cooks.' Lifting a hunk of the 'steak,' streaming ketchup, to his mouth, Winkelmann chewed. 'Just the thing,' he smiled.

units.claim: Bailey is upset by the Captain's use of ketchup on his creation.
units.evidence: Bailey shouted. 'Damn you!'

units.claim: The Captain demands that Bailey keep a bottle of ketchup on the table for his future meals.
units.evidence: Please keep a bottle on the table for all my future meals, Belly-Robber.

units.claim: The Captain warns that a dyspeptic Captain is a threat to the welfare of the ship.
units.evidence: a dyspeptic Captain is a threat to the welfare of his ship.

units.claim: The Captain threatens to not be in condition to land the ship safely if he continues eating Bailey's meals without ketchup.
units.evidence: Were I to continue eating your surrealistic slops for another hundred days, without the small consolation of this sauce I had the foresight to bring with me, I'd likely be in no condition to jet us safely down to the Piano West pad.

units.claim: The narrator tries to defend Bailey to the Captain.
units.evidence: Doctor, I must point out to you that it ill behooves the Ship's Surgeon to side with the Cook against the Captain,

units.claim: The Captain dismisses both Bailey and the narrator from the mess compartment.
units.evidence: Doctor, you are excused. As are you, Belly-Robber,

units.claim: Bailey cries and is given a drink by the narrator for therapy.
units.evidence: I poured us each some fifty cc's of rye. 'This is therapy, Bailey,' I told him.

units.claim: Bailey is angry at the Captain for expecting him to prepare complex dishes with limited resources.
units.evidence: What sane man would expect me to dip Wiener schnitzel and sauerkraut and Backhahndl nach suddeutscher Art out of an algae tank?

units.claim: Bailey is frustrated with the lack of appreciation for his efforts.
units.evidence: You've worked your fingers to the bone, slaving over a hot stove, and you're not appreciated.

units.claim: The narrator reassures Bailey that he will eventually be back home and able to start his own restaurant.
units.evidence: A year from now you'll be home in Ohio, fifty grand richer, set to start that restaurant of yours and forget about our fat Flying Dutchman.

units.claim: Bailey expresses hatred towards the Captain.
units.evidence: I hate him,

units.claim: The next day, the Captain compliments Bailey on the broth despite its horribleness.
units.evidence: Belly-Robber, you're improving a little at last.

units.claim: Bailey nods and smiles in response to the Captain's compliment.
units.evidence: Bailey nodded and smiled. 'Thank you, Sir,' he said.

units.claim: Linton laid down his steel fork beside the restaurant water glass.
units.evidence: Linton lay down his steel fork beside the massively solid transparency of the restaurant water glass.

units.claim: Linton thought he saw Rogers Snead at a nearby table.
units.evidence: 'Isn't that Rogers Snead at that table?' he heard himself say stupidly.

units.claim: Howell denied that the man was Rogers Snead.
units.evidence: 'Not at all. Somebody who looks like him. Twin brother. You know how it is. Snead's dead, don't you remember?'

units.claim: Howell reminded Linton that Rogers Snead was dead.
units.evidence: 'Snead's dead, don't you remember?'

units.claim: Linton observed the man who looked like Snead leaving the restaurant.
units.evidence: 'The man who isn't Snead is leaving,' Linton said, describing the scene over Howell's shoulder.

units.claim: Howell advised Linton not to approach the man who looked like Snead.
units.evidence: 'No,' Howell said, 'I wouldn't do that.'

units.claim: Linton mentioned that Snead attended Greta's funeral.
units.evidence: 'Snead came to Greta's funeral. It's the least I could do.'

units.claim: Howell suggested that the man who looked like Snead was not related to him.
units.evidence: 'Probably no relation to Snead at all. Somebody who looks like him.'

units.claim: Linton noticed the man who looked like Snead was practically running out of the restaurant.
units.evidence: 'He's practically running,' Linton said. 'He almost ran out of the restaurant.'

units.claim: A thick-bodied man at the next table commented on the man who looked like Linton's friend.
units.evidence: 'That fellow who just left looked like a friend of yours, huh?' the thick man said.

units.claim: Linton confirmed that his friend was dead.
units.evidence: 'Couldn't have been him, though,' Linton answered automatically. 'My friend's dead.'

units.claim: The thick-bodied man left the restaurant quickly after the conversation.
units.evidence: He plodded out of the place quickly.

units.claim: Howell expressed concern that Linton might have caused trouble for Snead.
units.evidence: 'Now you've probably got old Snead into trouble.'

units.claim: Linton insisted that Snead was dead.
units.evidence: 'Snead's dead,' Linton said.

units.claim: Howell implied that there might be a possibility of Snead being resurrected.
units.evidence: 'I suppose he might have been resurrected.'

units.claim: Linton had previously buried his wife, Greta.
units.evidence: He had buried his wife, or rather he had watched the two workmen scoop and shove dirt in on the sawdust-fresh pine box that held the coffin.

units.claim: Linton believed he had a genuine affection for Greta even after being released from the asylum.
units.evidence: Even after they had let him out of the asylum as cured, he still secretly believed he had known a genuine affection for her.

units.claim: Howell suggested that someone might have invented a way to bring dead people back to life.
units.evidence: 'You mean, somebody has invented a way to bring dead people back to life?'

units.claim: Howell claimed to be an honest businessman and not involved with resurrectionists.
units.evidence: 'I'm an honest businessman.'

units.claim: Linton expressed interest in finding a resurrectionist.
units.evidence: 'Tell me, Howell, where could I find a resurrectionist?'

units.claim: Howell refused to provide information about resurrectionists.
units.evidence: 'Frank, I don't have anything to do with that kind of people and if you're smart, you'll not either.'

units.claim: Howell left the restaurant after Linton yelled at him.
units.evidence: Howell threw money on the table with the same kind of disinterest as the thick-set man and stalked out.

units.claim: Linton thought he needed to hurry because it was Resurrection Day.
units.evidence: It's Resurrection Day!

units.claim: A doctor mentioned that Linton had been causing disturbances.
units.evidence: 'Well, well, Mr. Linton, we understand you've been causing disturbances.'

units.claim: Linton denied causing disturbances.
units.evidence: 'Not really,' Linton said modestly.

units.claim: Johnny was killed instantly in a traffic accident.
units.evidence: Traffic accident. Killed instantly.

units.claim: The speaker had the ability to resurrect someone.
units.evidence: Why didn't you have him resurrected the same way you did me?

units.claim: Resurrection is described as a risky and expensive process.
units.evidence: resurrection is a risky business and an expensive one.

units.claim: Premium prices are required for certain items during specific times, such as strawberries in February.
units.evidence: You have to pay premium prices for strawberries in February.

units.claim: Linton no longer has the money to pay for a resurrection of Johnny.
units.evidence: I no longer have the money to pay for a resurrection of Johnny.

units.claim: Greta believes bringing Johnny back would be monstrous.
units.evidence: It's monstrous. No one should do that. No one.

units.claim: Linton has borrowed on his insurance to the maximum extent.
units.evidence: I've borrowed on my insurance to the hilt.

units.claim: Linton's insurance will not pay out until he is buried.
units.evidence: It won't pay any more until I'm buried

units.claim: Linton can be resurrected after being buried.
units.evidence: then, of course, you can resurrect me.

units.claim: Greta feels sorry for Linton over the loss of Johnny.
units.evidence: Poor Johnny. He was such a good friend of yours. You must miss him. I'm so sorry for you.

units.claim: Linton has Greta as a consolation for losing Johnny.
units.evidence: I have you,

units.claim: Greta describes a place with acid baths, disposals, and chemical barrels.
units.evidence: There are foaming acid baths, great whale-toothed disposals, barrels of chemicals to quench death and smother decay.

units.claim: Linton perceives the place Greta describes as carnal.
units.evidence: It sounds carnal,

units.claim: Greta believes the place she describes is perfect for some purposes.
units.evidence: it's perfect for some things that have to be done.

units.claim: Greta's gaze settles on an ashtray stand.
units.evidence: settled somewhere, on something.

units.claim: Linton sees the ashtray stand as resembling a fanatic's idol.
units.evidence: an ashtray stand, looking vaguely like a fanatic's idol to a heathen religion on a pedestal.

units.claim: Greta attempts to hit Linton with the ashtray stand.
units.evidence: Greta hit the edge of the desk instead of him.

units.claim: Linton concludes Greta may have brain damage or cell deterioration.
units.evidence: Brain damage, he concluded nervously. Cell deterioration.

units.claim: Greta wants the insurance money.
units.evidence: I have to have that insurance money. It's hell!

units.claim: Linton understands Greta's intention and feels foolish and humiliated.
units.evidence: Linton understood immediately. He felt foolish, humiliated.

units.claim: Linton had previously resurrected a gold ring that turned his knuckles green.
units.evidence: No one must ever know. Linton twisted the stand away from his wife and watched her face in some appalled form of satisfaction as it registered horror and acceptance of the crumpled metal disk falling toward it.

units.claim: Linton kills Greta by splitting her head open.
units.evidence: He split her head open and watched her float to the floor.

units.claim: Linton notices a fine wire mesh and shiny little tabs under Greta's skin.
units.evidence: a fine wire mesh just below the skin and those shiny little tabs that looked like pictures of transistors in institutional advertising.

units.claim: Linton speculates that resurrection involves modifying bodies.
units.evidence: Yes, it seemed they had to automate and modify the bodies somewhat in resurrection.

units.claim: Linton questions whether the old bodies are used in resurrection.
units.evidence: Didn't the resurrectionists just destroy the old corpses and make androids, synthetic creatures, to take their place?

units.claim: Linton believes perception makes reality.
units.evidence: It was what you thought was real that made it so, not the other way around.

units.claim: Linton calls out that he has killed his wife.
units.evidence: I've killed my wife!

units.claim: Linton experiences pain in his neck that puts him to sleep.
units.evidence: The pain stung him to sleep—a pain in his neck like a needle that left a hole big enough for a camel to pass through and big enough for him to follow the camel in his turn.

units.claim: Linton wakes up in a doctor's office.
units.evidence: He opened his eyes to the doctor's spotless, well-ordered office.

units.claim: The doctor consoles Linton and tells him he will be cured.
units.evidence: You'll have to go back, Mr. Linton. But they'll cure you. You'll be cured of ever thinking your wife was brought back to life and that you killed her all over again.

units.claim: Linton hopes the doctor's prognosis is true.
units.evidence: Do you really think so, Doctor?

units.claim: The planet Mars is described as barren, desolate, and forbidding.
units.evidence: The planet itself was tough enough—barren, desolate, forbidding;

units.claim: There is an antagonist on Mars with the motto 'Death to all Terrans!'
units.evidence: But they had to run head-on against a mad genius who had a motto: Death to all Terrans!

units.claim: Ron tells Val to keep moving to avoid dying on Mars.
units.evidence: "Let's keep moving," I told Val. "The surest way to die out here on Mars is to give up."

units.claim: Ron adjusts Val's oxygen mask to make breathing easier.
units.evidence: I reached over and turned up the pressure on her oxymask to make things a little easier for her.

units.claim: Val is experiencing fatigue while walking on Mars.
units.evidence: Through the glassite of the mask, I could see her face contorted in an agony of fatigue.

units.claim: Val blames Ron for the failure of the sandcat vehicle.
units.evidence: And she probably thought the failure of the sandcat was all my fault, too.

units.claim: Ron believes the fault lies with someone at the Dome who failed to secure the engine hood.
units.evidence: But no; she blamed it all on me somehow: So we were out walking on the spongy sand of the Martian desert.

units.claim: Sand in the atomic engine mechanism can stop a sandcat vehicle.
units.evidence: Nothing but what had stopped us could stop a sandcat: sand in the delicate mechanism of the atomic engine.

units.claim: Ron and Val have been walking for eight hours on the Martian desert.
units.evidence: We'd been walking a good eight hours.

units.claim: Val pleads with Ron to turn back due to exhaustion.
units.evidence: "Can't we turn back now, Ron?" Val pleaded.

units.claim: Ron refrains from arguing with Val when she is tired and overwrought.
units.evidence: When Val's tired and overwrought there's no sense in arguing with her.

units.claim: Ron reminds Val that they are searching for uranium on Mars.
units.evidence: I started to tell her that the UranCo chief had assured me we'd hit something out this way, but changed my mind.

units.claim: Val complains about the pay from UranCo.
units.evidence: UranCo's pay is stinking.

units.claim: Ron and Val came to Mars to help Earth's industries with uranium.
units.evidence: We knew the pay was poor, but we had felt it a sort of obligation, something we could do as individuals to keep the industries of radioactives-starved Earth going.

units.claim: Val is at the breaking point due to exhaustion.
units.evidence: Now I knew she was at the breaking point, because Val didn't lie unless she was so exhausted she didn't know what she was doing.

units.claim: Ron feels guilty for bringing Val to Mars, but remembers she volunteered first.
units.evidence: I felt almost guilty for having dragged her out to Mars, until I recalled that I hadn't. In fact, she had come up with the idea before I did.

units.claim: Ron decides to rest before continuing their journey.
units.evidence: I think we ought to rest a little before we go any further. It's been a long, hard day.

units.claim: Val falls asleep quickly after resting.
units.evidence: She slid down beside me, curled up, and in a moment she was fast asleep, sprawled out on the sands.

units.claim: Ron reflects on their decision to come to Mars.
units.evidence: Maybe we shouldn't have come to Mars after all. But, I reminded myself, someone had to do the job.

units.claim: Ron watches Val sleeping and thinks about their life on Earth.
units.evidence: I watched her, sleeping peacefully, a wayward lock of her soft blonde hair trailing down over one eyebrow, and it seemed hard to believe that we'd exchanged Earth and all it held for us for the raw, untamed struggle that was Mars.

units.claim: Ron decides not to wake Val and continues to watch the desert.
units.evidence: But then Val stirred and rolled over in her sleep, and I didn't have the heart to wake her. I sat there, holding her, staring out over the desert, watching the wind whip the sand up into weird shapes.

units.claim: Earth needed radioactives.
units.evidence: Earth needed radioactives,

units.claim: The only way to get radioactives was to explore outside Earth.
units.evidence: and the only way to get them was to get out and look.

units.claim: The great atomic wars of the late 20th Century had used up much of the supply of radioactives.
units.evidence: The great atomic wars of the late 20th Century had used up much of the supply,

units.claim: The amount of radioactives used to destroy cities was less than what was needed to rebuild them.
units.evidence: but the amount used to blow up half the great cities of the world hardly compared with the amount we needed to put them back together again.

units.claim: In three centuries, the shattered world had been completely rebuilt.
units.evidence: In three centuries the shattered world had been completely rebuilt.

units.claim: New York, Shanghai, and London were rebuilt after being ruined.
units.evidence: The wreckage of New York and Shanghai and London and all the other ruined cities had been hidden by a shining new world of gleaming towers and flying roadways.

units.claim: The rebuilt world used radioactives for fuel instead of bombs.
units.evidence: They had used their atomics to make bombs. We used ours for fuel.

units.claim: Everything in the rebuilt world was powered by atomic energy.
units.evidence: It was an atomic world. Everything: power drills, printing presses, typewriters, can openers, ocean liners, powered by the inexhaustible energy of the dividing atom.

units.claim: The supply of atomic nuclei was running out after three centuries of heavy consumption.
units.evidence: But though the energy is inexhaustible, the supply of nuclei isn't. After three centuries of heavy consumption, the supply failed.

units.claim: Earth's industry started to slow down due to the lack of atomic nuclei.
units.evidence: The mighty machine that was Earth's industry had started to slow down.

units.claim: Project Sea-Dredge aimed to obtain uranium from the oceans.
units.evidence: Project Sea-Dredge was trying to get uranium from the oceans.

units.claim: Project Sea-Dredge would take forty or fifty years to yield results.
units.evidence: In forty or fifty years, they'd get some results, we hoped.

units.claim: There wasn't enough uranium to last until Project Sea-Dredge started functioning.
units.evidence: But there wasn't forty or fifty years' worth of raw stuff to tide us over until then.

units.claim: Without uranium, the world would revert to a dog-eat-dog state.
units.evidence: Millions of starving, freezing humans tooth-and-clawing in it in the useless shell of a great atomic civilization.

units.claim: Mars was explored for uranium deposits.
units.evidence: So, Mars. There's not much uranium on Mars, and it's not easy to find or any cinch to mine. But what little is there, helps.

units.claim: The Geig Corps were volunteers searching for uranium deposits on Mars.
units.evidence: Enter the Geig Corps: volunteers out on the face of Mars, combing for its uranium deposits.

units.claim: Gregory Ledman was a man who hated.
units.evidence: His face was a bitter, dried-up mask. He was a man who hated.

units.claim: Ledman's Dome was sparsely furnished.
units.evidence: The place was spartanly furnished. No chairs, no tape-player, no decoration of any sort.

units.claim: Ledman intended to kill the Geigs and drive them off Mars.
units.evidence: Because I hate you,

units.claim: He didn't smile this time.
units.evidence: He didn't smile this time.

units.claim: He told her he wanted to kill her.
units.evidence: "Kill you," he told her.

units.claim: He did not intend to kill her husband.
units.evidence: Not your husband.

units.claim: He intended to use her husband as an envoy.
units.evidence: I want him as an envoy, to go back and tell the others to clear off.

units.claim: He was rocking back and forth in his wheelchair.
units.evidence: He rocked back and forth in his wheelchair

units.claim: He was holding a blaster.
units.evidence: toying with the gleaming, deadly blaster in his hand.

units.claim: They stared in horror at him.
units.evidence: We stared in horror.

units.claim: He asked if he shocked them.
units.evidence: "Do I shock you?" he asked.

units.claim: He claimed they should not be shocked given their understanding of his motives.
units.evidence: I shouldn't—not when you see my motives.

units.claim: They responded that they did not see his motives.
units.evidence: "We don't see them," I snapped.

units.claim: He mentioned they were on Mars hunting uranium.
units.evidence: Well, let me show you. You're on Mars hunting uranium, right?

units.claim: Their purpose was to mine and ship radioactives back to Earth.
units.evidence: To mine and ship the radioactives back to Earth to keep the atomic engines going.

units.claim: Val stated they volunteered to come to Mars.
units.evidence: "We volunteered to come to Mars," Val said irrelevantly.

units.claim: Ledman sarcastically referred to them as two young heroes.
units.evidence: "Ah—two young heroes," Ledman said acidly.

units.claim: Ledman mentioned the Sadlerville Blast.
units.evidence: Atomics cost me my legs, he said. "You remember the Sadlerville Blast?" he asked.

units.claim: The Sadlerville Blast killed hundreds and injured thousands.
units.evidence: No one would. How could I forget that great accident—killing hundreds, injuring thousands more, sterilizing forty miles of Mississippi land—when the Sadlerville pile went up?

units.claim: Ledman was at Sadlerville on business representing Ledman Atomics.
units.evidence: I was there on business at the time, Ledman said. I represented Ledman Atomics.

units.claim: Ledman was supposed to sign a new contract for his company.
units.evidence: I was there to sign a new contract for my company.

units.claim: Ledman received a dose of radiation during the blast.
units.evidence: I never got the contract, but I got a good dose of radiation instead.

units.claim: Ledman's radiation dose necessitated the removal of his legs.
units.evidence: Just enough to necessitate the removal of—

units.claim: Ledman became a pauper after losing his company.
units.evidence: All quite legal, I assure you. They left me almost a pauper!

units.claim: Ledman's company was renamed.
units.evidence: They renamed Ledman Atomics.

units.claim: Ledman saved money and came to Mars to build a dome.
units.evidence: I saved for years; then I came to Mars, lost myself, built this Dome, and swore to get even.

units.claim: Ledman planned to get even with those who took away his legs.
units.evidence: But I'll pay it all back.

units.claim: Ledman needed regular injections due to the blast.
units.evidence: He consulted his wrist watch. "Time for my injection."

units.claim: Ledman was short on red blood corpuscles.
units.evidence: I'm short on red blood corpuscles.

units.claim: Ledman had to take various injections including adrenalin and insulin.
units.evidence: There are other injections, too. Adrenalin, insulin. Others.

units.claim: Ledman believed meddling with atoms led to his condition.
units.evidence: If we hadn't meddled with the atom in the first place, I'd be as tall and powerful as you, today—instead of a useless cripple in a wheelchair.

units.claim: Val called Ledman sick and insane.
units.evidence: "You're sick, Gregory Ledman," Val said quietly. "You've conceived an impossible scheme of revenge and now you're taking it out on innocent people who've done nothing, nothing at all to you. That's not sane!"

units.claim: Ledman was angry at being called insane.
units.evidence: His eyes blazed. "Who are you to talk of sanity?"

units.claim: Val was sweating profusely.
units.evidence: Sweat was rolling down her smooth forehead faster than the auto-wiper could swab it away.

units.claim: Ron told Val to pretend to be sick.
units.evidence: "Get sick!" I hissed to Val, low.

units.claim: Val pretended to be unable to breathe.
units.evidence: She began immediately to cough violently, emitting harsh, choking sobs. "Can't breathe!" She began to yell, writhing in her bonds.

units.claim: Ledman lowered his blaster and approached Val.
units.evidence: He lowered the blaster a bit and wheeled one-hand over to see what was wrong with Val.

units.claim: Ron kicked Ledman's wheelchair over.
units.evidence: I snapped my leg up hard, tearing the tangle-cord with a snicking rasp, and kicked his wheelchair over.

units.claim: Ledman had little humanity left in him.
units.evidence: Ledman hadn't much humanity left in him,

units.claim: Ledman lowered the blaster and checked on Val.
units.evidence: He lowered the blaster a bit and wheeled one-hand over to see what was wrong with Val.

units.claim: Val was retching and moaning horribly.
units.evidence: She continued to retch and moan most horribly.

units.claim: Val's face showed fear and turned towards the speaker.
units.evidence: I saw Val's pale, frightened face turn to me.

units.claim: The speaker kicked Ledman's wheelchair over.
units.evidence: I snapped my leg up hard, tearing the tangle-cord with a snicking rasp, and kicked his wheelchair over.

units.claim: The blaster fired and burned a hole through the Dome roof.
units.evidence: The blaster went off, burning a hole through the Dome roof.

units.claim: Automatic sealers sealed the hole in the Dome roof.
units.evidence: The automatic sealers glued-in instantly.

units.claim: Ledman fell helplessly onto the floor.
units.evidence: Ledman went sprawling helplessly out into the middle of the floor.

units.claim: The blaster flew out near the speaker.
units.evidence: The blaster flew from his hands at the impact of landing and spun out near me.

units.claim: The speaker covered the blaster with their body.
units.evidence: In one quick motion I rolled over and covered it with my body.

units.claim: Ledman tried to pry the blaster out from under the speaker but failed.
units.evidence: Ledman clawed his way to me with tremendous effort and tried wildly to pry the blaster out from under me, but without success.

units.claim: The speaker kicked Ledman across the floor.
units.evidence: I twisted a bit, reached out with my free leg, and booted him across the floor.

units.claim: Ledman hit the wall and lay there.
units.evidence: He fetched up against the wall of the Dome and lay there.

units.claim: Val rolled over to the speaker.
