units.evidence: Ggaran stepped out into the broad corridor and whistled a shrill two-tone note, using both his speaking and his eating orifices.

units.claim: A cohort of troops forms a double line from His Effulgence's sanctum to the main door.
units.evidence: A cohort of troops, pikes at the ready and bows strapped to their backs, leaped forward and formed a double line leading from His Effulgence's sanctum to the main door.

units.claim: A large sedan chair is carried by twenty men.
units.evidence: Down this lane, carried by twenty men, came a large sedan chair.

units.claim: Crownwall rides in the sedan chair with Ffallk.
units.evidence: I'm glad of that,

units.claim: The sedan chair is carried at seven or eight kilometers an hour.
units.evidence: The bearers trotted along at seven or eight kilometers an hour

units.claim: No one is allowed to watch when the Viceroy of the Seventy Suns travels in state.
units.evidence: When the Viceroy of the Seventy Suns travels in state, no one but my own entourage is permitted to watch.

units.claim: Ggaran demonstrates the consequences of violating the tradition of clearing the streets.
units.evidence: Let us just suppose that that runner over there is a civilian who has been so unlucky as to remain on the street after His Effulgence's entourage arrived.

units.claim: A bowman kills a soldier with an arrow.
units.evidence: The arrow hissed briefly, and then sliced smoothly through the soldier's throat.

units.claim: His Effulgence criticizes the bowman's technique.
units.evidence: Your results were satisfactory, but your release was somewhat shaky. The next time you show such sloppy form, you will be given thirty lashes.

units.claim: His Effulgence believes that modern weapons should not be used on ceremonial occasions.
units.evidence: It would never do for them to use modern weapons on occasions of ceremony, of course.

units.claim: Crownwall suggests providing live targets more often for practice.
units.evidence: It's too bad that you can't provide them with live targets a little more often.

units.claim: Crownwall feels disgust at the demonstration.
units.evidence: He stifled a shudder of distaste.

units.claim: His Effulgence believes the Emperor's race is too brutal to understand etiquette.
units.evidence: They are far too brutal, too morally degraded, to know anything of these finer points of etiquette and propriety.

units.claim: His Effulgence believes the Emperor's race would use an energy weapon in the demonstrated situation.
units.evidence: Why, do you know, I am certain that they would have had the bad taste to use an energy weapon to dispose of the victim in a case such as you just witnessed!

units.claim: His Effulgence believes the Emperor's race is unfit to rule.
units.evidence: They are really quite unfit to rule.

units.claim: Crownwall hopes to improve the situation with the Emperor's race.
units.evidence: I sincerely hope so,

units.claim: Refreshments are served to His Effulgence and Crownwall during the trip.
units.evidence: Refreshments were served to His Effulgence and to Crownwall during the trip

units.claim: The soldiers continue to run without food, drink, or visible signs of fatigue.
units.evidence: The soldiers of the cohort, the bearers and Ggaran continued to run—without food, drink or, except for Ggaran, evidence of fatigue.

units.claim: Crownwall arrives at the copse where his transportation machine is hidden.
units.evidence: the procession arrived at the copse in which he had concealed his small transportation machine.

units.claim: Crownwall's machine uses a heavy and inefficient anti-gravity field generator.
units.evidence: It occupied ten times the space of the temporal translation and coordination selection systems combined, but it had the great advantage of being almost undetectable in use.

units.claim: Crownwall's machine emits no mass or radiation.
units.evidence: It emitted no mass or radiation.

units.claim: Crownwall returns to Earth to make a full report on his trip to Vega.
units.evidence: he was in the Council Chamber of the Confederation Government of Earth, making a full report on his trip to Vega.

units.claim: The President expresses concern about the treaty with the Vegans.
units.evidence: But from what you say, I'd rather be in bed with a rattler than have a treaty with a Vegan.

units.claim: The President believes the Vegans are murderous.
units.evidence: They sound ungodly murderous to me.

units.claim: The President believes there are too many holes in the protection plan.
units.evidence: There are too many holes in that protection plan of yours.

units.claim: The President believes the Vegans will eventually find a way around the protection plan.
units.evidence: It's only a question of time before they'll find some way around it, and then—poof—we'll all be dust.

units.claim: The sand-thing was described as powerful, lonely, and strange.
units.evidence: The sand-thing was powerful, lonely and strange.

units.claim: Stinson believed the sand-thing may be a god.
units.evidence: No doubt it was a god—but who wasn't?

units.claim: Stinson lay still in the sand after his arrival.
units.evidence: Stinson lay still in the sand where he fell, gloating over the success of his arrival.

units.claim: Stinson had a pencil-line scar behind his ear where a cylinder was buried.
units.evidence: He touched the pencil-line scar behind his ear where the cylinder was buried

units.claim: The cylinder contained power to transport Stinson instantly from Earth to the fourth planet of the Centaurian system.
units.evidence: marveling at the power stored there, power to fling him from earth to this fourth planet of the Centaurian system in an instant.

units.claim: Stinson could almost feel the warm, humid Missouri air despite being light years away.
units.evidence: though he was light years from Missouri.

units.claim: Stinson observed a gray, funnel-shaped cloud of dust to his left.
units.evidence: A gray, funnel-shaped cloud of dust stood off to his left.

units.claim: The cloud did not move except to spin on its axis rapidly and emit a high-pitched whine.
units.evidence: This became disturbing, since there was scarcely enough wind to move his hair. He watched it, trying to recall what he might know about cyclones. But he knew little. Weather control made cyclones and other climatic phenomena on earth practically non-existent. The cloud did not move, though, except to spin on its axis rapidly, emitting a high-pitched, scarcely audible whine, like a high speed motor.

units.claim: Stinson judged the cloud to be harmless.
units.evidence: He judged it harmless.

units.claim: Stinson stood on a wide valley floor between two mountain ranges.
units.evidence: He stood on a wide valley floor between two mountain ranges.

units.claim: Dark clouds capped one peak of the mountains on Stinson's left.
units.evidence: Dark clouds capped one peak of the mountains on his left.

units.claim: The sky was deep blue.
units.evidence: The sky was deep blue.

units.claim: Stinson tested the gravity and found it to be the same as Earth's gravity.
units.evidence: He tested the gravity by jumping up and down. Same as Earth gravity.

units.claim: Stinson realized he was on a planet in the Centaurian system.
units.evidence: Not Sol. What should he call it, Alpha or Centaurus? Well, perhaps neither. He was here and Earth was somewhere up there. This was the sun of this particular solar system. He was right the first time.

units.claim: The sun burned fiercely, even though it appeared to be around four o'clock in the afternoon.
units.evidence: The sun burned fiercely, although he would have said it was about four o'clock in the afternoon, if this had been Earth.

units.claim: The landscape was entirely desert.
units.evidence: Not a tree, nor a bush, nor even a wisp of dry grass was in sight. Everywhere was desert.

units.claim: The funnel of sand moved closer to Stinson.
units.evidence: The funnel of sand had moved closer and while he watched it, it seemed to drift in the wind—although there was no wind.

units.claim: The funnel of sand changed shape, becoming a blue rectangle, a red cube, and a violet sphere.
units.evidence: It was about ten feet tall by three feet in diameter at the base. Then Stinson backed away. It was changing. Now it became a blue rectangle, then a red cube, a violet sphere.

units.claim: Stinson wished Benjamin were present to explain the phenomenon.
units.evidence: He wished Benjamin were here. Ben might have an explanation.

units.claim: Stinson turned his back and walked away from the funnel of sand.
units.evidence: He turned his back and walked away.

units.claim: The funnel of sand followed Stinson wherever he went.
units.evidence: When he looked up the wind devil was there before him. He looked back. Only one. It had moved.

units.claim: The funnel of sand cast a faint shadow.
units.evidence: The wind devil also had a shadow, although the sun shone through it and the shadow was faint.

units.claim: Stinson tried to communicate with the funnel of sand by drawing shapes in the sand.
units.evidence: He smoothed a place in the sand and drew a triangle with his forefinger. When it changed to a cube he drew a square, a circle for a sphere, and so on.

units.claim: Stinson inhaled grains of sand and projected himself a thousand miles away.
units.evidence: Instantly he projected himself a thousand miles away.

units.claim: Stinson arrived in an area of profuse vegetation.
units.evidence: Now he was in an area of profuse vegetation.

units.claim: It was twilight when Stinson arrived in the new location.
units.evidence: It was twilight.

units.claim: A chill wind blew from the northwest.
units.evidence: As he stood beside a small creek, a chill wind blew from the northwest.

units.claim: Stinson found dry and brittle leaves.
units.evidence: he found, but they were dry and brittle, for here autumn had turned the leaves.

units.claim: Night would be cold.
units.evidence: Night would be cold.

units.claim: Stinson followed the creek to where it flowed between two great hills.
units.evidence: So he followed the creek to where it flowed between two great hills.

units.claim: Steam vapors rose from a crevice near the creek.
units.evidence: Steam vapors rose from a crevice.

units.claim: Stinson entered a nearby cave with warm air flowing from its mouth.
units.evidence: A cave was nearby and warm air flowed from its mouth. He went inside.

units.claim: The cave initially appeared small but led to a long narrow passageway.
units.evidence: At first he thought the cave was small, but found instead that he was in a long narrow passageway.

units.claim: Warm air flowed through the passageway.
units.evidence: The current of warm air flowed toward him and he followed it, cautiously, stepping carefully and slowly.

units.claim: The passageway led to a large cavern with a high-vaulted ceiling.
units.evidence: Soon he stepped out of the narrow passageway into a great cavern with a high-vaulted ceiling.

units.claim: A great crystal sphere hung from the ceiling of the cavern.
units.evidence: A great crystal sphere hung from the ceiling, and he was curious about its purpose, but a great pool of steaming water in the center of the cavern drew his attention.

units.claim: A great pool of steaming water was in the center of the cavern.
units.evidence: A great pool of steaming water in the center of the cavern drew his attention.

units.claim: The stone wall surrounding the pool was inscribed with intricate artwork and indecipherable symbols.
units.evidence: A stone wall surrounding the pool was inscribed with intricate art work and indecipherable symbols.

units.claim: Stinson concluded the planet was inhabited.
units.evidence: Life. Intelligence. The planet was inhabited.

units.claim: Stinson considered whether to give up and return to Earth or stay to see if there was room for his people.
units.evidence: Should he give up and return to earth? Or was there room here for his people?

units.claim: Stinson thought of Benjamin, Straus, and Jamieson, who were struggling for life against those who desired them.
units.evidence: He thought of Benjamin, and Straus, and Jamieson—all those to whom he had given cylinders, and who were now struggling for life against those who desired them.

units.claim: Stinson decided it would not be just to give up so easily.
units.evidence: He decided it would not be just, to give up so easily.

units.claim: The wide plaza between the pool and cavern wall was smooth as polished glass.
units.evidence: The wide plaza between the pool and cavern wall was smooth as polished glass.

units.claim: Statues lined the wall of the cavern.
units.evidence: Statues lined the wall. He examined them.

units.claim: From one angle, the statues resembled animals.
units.evidence: From one angle they were animals,

units.claim: From another angle, the statues resembled birds.
units.evidence: from another birds,

units.claim: From a third angle, the statues resembled vaguely humanoid creatures.
units.evidence: from a third they were vaguely humanoid creatures, glowering at him with primitive ferocity.

units.claim: The fourth view of the statues was shocking and undefined.
units.evidence: The fourth view was so shocking he had to turn away quickly. No definable form or sculptured line was visible, yet he felt, or saw—he did not know which senses told him—the immeasurable gulf of a million years of painful evolution. Then nothing. It was not a curtain drawn to prevent him from seeing more.

units.claim: Stinson stumbled toward the pool's wall and clutched for support.
units.evidence: He stumbled toward the pool's wall and clutched for support, but his knees buckled.

units.claim: Stinson's hand slid down the wall over ancient inscriptions.
units.evidence: his hand slid down the wall, over the ancient inscriptions.

units.claim: Stinson sank to the floor before losing consciousness.
units.evidence: He sank to the floor. Before he lost consciousness he wondered, fleetingly, if a lethal instrument was in the statue.

units.claim: Stinson woke with a ringing in his ears, feeling drugged and sluggish.
units.evidence: He woke with a ringing in his ears, feeling drugged and sluggish.

units.claim: Stinson heard sounds after waking.
units.evidence: Sounds came to him. He opened his eyes.

units.claim: There was no more.
units.evidence: There was no more.

units.claim: He stumbled toward the pool's wall and clutched for support, but his knees buckled.
units.evidence: He stumbled toward the pool's wall and clutched for support, but his knees buckled.

units.claim: His hand slid down the wall, over the ancient inscriptions.
units.evidence: His hand slid down the wall, over the ancient inscriptions.

units.claim: He sank to the floor.
units.evidence: He sank to the floor.

units.claim: Before he lost consciousness, he wondered if a lethal instrument was in the statue.
units.evidence: Before he lost consciousness he wondered, fleetingly, if a lethal instrument was in the statue.

units.claim: He woke with a ringing in his ears, feeling drugged and sluggish.
units.evidence: He woke with a ringing in his ears, feeling drugged and sluggish.

units.claim: Sounds came to him.
units.evidence: Sounds came to him.

units.claim: He opened his eyes.
units.evidence: He opened his eyes.

units.claim: The cavern was crowded.
units.evidence: The cavern was crowded.

units.claim: These creatures were not only humanoid, but definitely human, although more slight of build than earth people.
units.evidence: These creatures were not only humanoid, but definitely human, although more slight of build than earth people.

units.claim: The only difference he could see at first sight was that they had webbed feet.
units.evidence: The only difference he could see at first sight was that they had webbed feet.

units.claim: All were dressed from the waist down only, in a shimmering skirt that sparkled as they moved.
units.evidence: All were dressed from the waist down only, in a shimmering skirt that sparkled as they moved.

units.claim: They walked with the grace of ballet dancers, moving about the plaza, conversing in a musical language with no meaning for Stinson.
units.evidence: They walked with the grace of ballet dancers, moving about the plaza, conversing in a musical language with no meaning for Stinson.

units.claim: The men were dark-skinned, the women somewhat lighter, with long flowing hair, wide lips and a beauty that was utterly sensual.
units.evidence: The men were dark-skinned, the women somewhat lighter, with long flowing hair, wide lips and a beauty that was utterly sensual.

units.claim: He was in chains!
units.evidence: He was in chains!

units.claim: The chains were small, lightweight, made of a metal that looked like aluminum.
units.evidence: They were small chains, light weight, of a metal that looked like aluminum.

units.claim: All his strength could not break the chains.
units.evidence: But all his strength could not break them.

units.claim: Two of the men came over and spoke to him in the musical language.
units.evidence: They saw him struggling. Two of the men came over and spoke to him in the musical language.

units.claim: Stinson introduced himself and mentioned he was from the planet Earth.
units.evidence: "My name is Stinson," he said, pointing to himself. "I'm from the planet Earth."

units.claim: The creatures looked at each other and jabbered some more.
units.evidence: They looked at each other and jabbered some more.

units.claim: Stinson tried to explain Earth by describing circles and showing how Earth revolves around the sun.
units.evidence: "Look," he said, "Earth. E-A-R-T-H, Earth." He pointed upward, described a large circle, then another smaller, and showed how Earth revolved around the sun.

units.claim: One of the men poked Stinson with a stick or tube, which did not hurt but angered him.
units.evidence: One of the men poked him with a stick, or tube of some kind. It did not hurt, but angered him.

units.claim: Stinson escaped his chains by his own method of travel and reappeared behind the two men.
units.evidence: He left the chains by his own method of travel, and reappeared behind the two men.

units.claim: Stinson slapped the face of the man who poked him.
units.evidence: He grasped the shoulder of the offender, spun him around and slapped his face.

units.claim: A cry of consternation rose from the group, echoing in the high ceilinged cavern.
units.evidence: A cry of consternation rose from the group, echoing in the high ceilinged cavern.

units.claim: The creatures prostrated themselves before Stinson.
units.evidence: The men instantly prostrated themselves before him.

units.claim: The man who poked Stinson with the stick rose and handed it to him.
units.evidence: The one who had poked Stinson with the stick rose, and handed it to him.

units.claim: As Stinson grasped the tube, a flash of blue fire sprang from it, disintegrating the man.
units.evidence: As he did so, a flash of blue fire sprang from it. The man disappeared. A small cloud of dust settled slowly to the floor.

units.claim: Stinson was ashamed because he had no clothes.
units.evidence: Disintegrated! Stinson's face drained pale, and suddenly, unaccountably, he was ashamed because he had no clothes.

units.claim: Stinson claimed he did not mean to kill the man.
units.evidence: "I didn't mean to kill him!" he cried. "I was angry, and...."

units.claim: The creatures could not understand Stinson.
units.evidence: Useless. They could not understand.

units.claim: The object Stinson thought was a stick was actually a long metal tube with a small button near one end.
units.evidence: The object he had thought of as a stick was in reality a long metal tube, precisely machined, with a small button near one end.

units.claim: The weapon was out of place in the culture.
units.evidence: This weapon was completely out of place in a culture such as this.

units.claim: The creatures exhibited human emotions of anger, fear, and curiosity.
units.evidence: They were humanoid. They had exhibited human emotions of anger, fear and, that most human of all characteristics, curiosity.

units.claim: The only evidence of advanced technology was the tube and the chain.
units.evidence: But up to now the tube and the chain was the only evidence of an advanced technology, unless the ancient inscriptions in the stone wall of the pool, and the statues lining the wall were evidences.

units.claim: An object like a pallet was brought by four women and laid at Stinson's feet.
units.evidence: There was a stirring among the crowd. An object like a pallet was brought, carried by four of the women. They laid it at his feet, and gestured for him to sit.

units.claim: Stinson touched the pallet cautiously, then sat.
units.evidence: He touched it cautiously, then sat.

units.claim: Stinson sprang to his feet upon seeing the wind devil at the cavern entrance.
units.evidence: Instantly he sprang to his feet. There, at the cavern entrance, the wind devil writhed and undulated in a brilliant harmony of colors.

units.claim: A woman approached Stinson, pressed her body against him, and bore him to the pallet.
units.evidence: One of the women came toward him, long golden hair flowing, firm breasts dipping slightly at each step. Her eyes held a language all their own, universal. She pressed her body against him and bore him to the pallet, her kisses fire on his face.

units.claim: Stinson thought of Benjamin and others back on Earth who might be fighting for their lives.
units.evidence: Incongruously, he thought of Benjamin back on earth, and all the others with cylinders, who might be fighting for their lives at this moment.

units.claim: Stinson pushed the woman roughly aside.
units.evidence: He pushed her roughly aside.

units.claim: Stinson understood the woman's words due to the wind devil.
units.evidence: She spoke, and he understood! Her words were still the same gibberish, but now he knew their meaning. Somehow he knew also that the wind devil was responsible for his understanding.

units.claim: The woman expressed sadness that Stinson did not want her.
units.evidence: "You do not want me?" she said sadly.

units.claim: The woman suggested Stinson should kill her.
units.evidence: "Then kill me."

units.claim: Stinson questioned why he should kill the woman.
units.evidence: "Why should I kill you?"

units.claim: The woman explained that it was the way of the Gods.
units.evidence: She shrugged her beautiful shoulders. "It is the way of the Gods," she said. "If you do not, then the others will."

units.claim: Stinson promised to protect the woman.
units.evidence: "Don't be afraid. I didn't mean to kill the man. It was an accident. I will protect you."

units.claim: The woman believed the others would eventually kill her.
units.evidence: She shook her head. "One day they will find me alone, and they'll kill me."

units.claim: Stinson explained there was a time and place for everything.
units.evidence: "On the contrary, you have. There is a time and place for everything, though."

units.claim: A great voice sounded in the cavern, coming from multiple directions.
units.evidence: Suddenly a great voice sounded in the cavern, a voice with no direction. It came from the ceiling, the floor, the walls, the steaming pool.

units.claim: The voice instructed that no harm must come to the woman.
units.evidence: "No harm must come to this woman. The God with fingers on his feet has decreed this."

units.claim: The creatures looked at the woman with fear and respect.
units.evidence: Those in the cavern looked at the woman with fear and respect.

units.claim: The woman kissed Stinson's feet.
units.evidence: She kissed Stinson's feet.

units.claim: Two men gave the woman a brilliant new skirt.
units.evidence: Two of the men came and gave her a brilliant new skirt.

units.claim: The woman smiled at Stinson.
units.evidence: She smiled at him, and he thought he had never seen a more beautiful face.

units.claim: The great voice sounded again, but the creatures continued their activities.
units.evidence: The great, bodiless voice sounded again, but those in the cavern went about their activities. They did not hear.

units.claim: Stinson asked who was speaking.
units.evidence: "Who are you?"

units.claim: Stinson pointed to himself and asked if the voice meant him.
units.evidence: Stinson looked at the wind devil, since it could be no one else speaking, and pointed to himself. "Me?"

units.claim: The voice confirmed it was addressing Stinson.
units.evidence: "Yes."

units.claim: Stinson identified himself as Stinson from the planet Earth.
units.evidence: "I am Stinson, of the planet Earth."

units.claim: The voice stated that Stinson wanted to live on the planet.
units.evidence: "You want to live here, on this planet."

units.claim: The voice asked how Stinson came to the planet.
units.evidence: Then you must know where I came from, and how.

units.claim: The voice did not understand how Stinson arrived physically.
units.evidence: I do not understand how. You have a body, a physical body composed of atoms. It is impossible to move a physical body from one place to another by a mere thought and a tiny instrument, yet you have done so.

units.claim: The voice accused Stinson of deserting it in the desert.
units.evidence: You deserted me out in the desert.

units.claim: Stinson denied deserting the voice.
units.evidence: "I deserted you?" Stinson cried angrily, "You tried to kill me!"

units.claim: The voice claimed it was attempting communication.
units.evidence: "I was attempting communication. Why should I kill you?"

units.claim: Stinson speculated the voice feared he would become the God of the people.
units.evidence: He was silent a moment, looking at the people in the cavern. "Perhaps because you feared I would become the God of these people in your place."

units.claim: Stinson introduces himself to a woman they are in trouble with.
units.evidence: "My name is Stinson."

units.claim: The woman introduces herself as Sybtl.
units.evidence: "I am Sybtl," she said.

units.claim: Stinson tries to pronounce Sybtl's name as 'Syb-tl'.
units.evidence: "Syb-tl." He tried to imitate her musical pronunciation.

units.claim: Sybtl warns Stinson that when the ice melts, others will follow them.
units.evidence: "When the ice is gone, they will come out and follow us."

units.claim: Stinson suggests they should leave quickly.
units.evidence: "We'd better make tracks."

units.claim: Sybtl insists they must run and make no tracks.
units.evidence: "No," she said, "we must run, and make no tracks."

units.claim: Stinson calls Sybtl 'Sis', meaning 'sister'.
units.evidence: "That means, sister."

units.claim: Sybtl corrects Stinson, stating she is his wife.
units.evidence: "I am not your sister. I am your wife."

units.claim: Stinson denies being a god and clarifies that Sybtl is not his wife.
units.evidence: "Listen, Sybtl," he said desperately, "I am not a God and you are not my wife. Let's get that straight."

units.claim: Stinson doubts the wisdom of keeping Sybtl with him due to the webfoots.
units.evidence: He doubted the wisdom of keeping her with him.

units.claim: Stinson feels strong knowing Sybtl depends on him.
units.evidence: He felt strong knowing she depended on him.

units.claim: Stinson and Sybtl run, slide, fall, and continue running.
units.evidence: He took her hand and they ran, slid, fell, picked themselves up again, and ran.

units.claim: Stinson thinks about using his cylinder to move to a safer location.
units.evidence: He glanced down at Sybtl and remembered the webfoots. He stopped, tempted to use his cylinder and move to a warmer, less dangerous spot.

units.claim: Sybtl urges Stinson to hurry.
units.evidence: The woman pulled on his arm. "We must hurry!"

units.claim: Stinson asks Sybtl how many times he can use the tube-weapon.
units.evidence: "How many shots in this thing?"

units.claim: Sybtl explains the tube-weapon can be used as often as needed for fifty years.
units.evidence: As often as you like. It is good for fifty years.

units.claim: Sybtl mentions Kaatr brought the tube-weapon from the ship ten years ago.
units.evidence: Kaatr—he is the one you destroyed—brought it from the ship when we came. Many times he has used it unwisely.

units.claim: Sybtl states that criminals and their children are brought to this planet.
units.evidence: Criminals, and their children.

units.claim: Sybtl's people have disowned her and those in the cavern.
units.evidence: They are no longer my people. They have disowned us.

units.claim: Stinson realizes the webfoots are approaching.
units.evidence: There, directly in their path, stood the Sand God. It was blood red now. It pulsed violently.

units.claim: The Sand God demands Stinson leave Sybtl.
units.evidence: "Leave the woman!" it demanded angrily.

units.claim: The Sand God warns Stinson that the webfoots are near.
units.evidence: The webfoots are nearing your position.

units.claim: Stinson refuses to leave Sybtl.
units.evidence: Stinson shook his head.

units.claim: The Sand God becomes angry and melts ice around it.
units.evidence: The Sand God pulsed more violently than before. Ice melted in a wide area around it.

units.claim: The Sand God criticizes Stinson's primitive logic.
units.evidence: What form of primitive stupidity are you practicing now?

units.claim: The Sand God threatens to destroy Stinson and his people if they return.
units.evidence: If you bring your people here, I shall destroy you all.

units.claim: The Sand God leaves, causing a loud noise and shaking the ground.
units.evidence: The sphere of blue fire screamed away across the frozen wilderness, and the thunder of its passing shook the ground and echoed among the lonely hills.

units.claim: Sybtl recalls the Sand God's previous actions against her people.
units.evidence: She touched her fingers on his face. "I am sorry. It was all for me."

units.claim: Stinson decides they are better off on Earth.
units.evidence: Well, Stinson said to himself, that does it. We are better off on Earth.

units.claim: Stinson and Sybtl enter a small cave for shelter.
units.evidence: They climbed the canyon wall. Far away, small figures moved. The webfoots were on their trail.

units.claim: The small cave is warm and provides a good vantage point.
units.evidence: It was heated, like the great cavern, but held no walled pool nor mysterious lighting. But it was warm, and the small entrance made an excellent vantage point for warding off attack.

units.claim: Someone asks if the other person knows where they came from and how.
units.evidence: "Then you must know where I came from, and how."

units.claim: The speaker does not understand how the other person moved physically from one place to another using just a thought and a small device.
units.evidence: "I do not understand how. You have a body, a physical body composed of atoms. It is impossible to move a physical body from one place to another by a mere thought and a tiny instrument, yet you have done so."

units.claim: The speaker accuses the other person of abandoning them in the desert.
units.evidence: "You deserted me out in the desert."

units.claim: Stinson denies having abandoned the speaker.
units.evidence: "I deserted you?" Stinson cried angrily, "You tried to kill me!"

units.claim: The speaker claims they were trying to communicate and not to kill Stinson.
units.evidence: "I was attempting communication. Why should I kill you?"

units.evidence: Kroger said that the Martian metabolism must be like Terran (Earth-type) metabolism, only with no pancreas to make insulin. They store their energy on the outside of their bodies, in the form of scales. He's watched them more closely and seen that they have long rubbery tubes for tongues, and that they now and then suck up water from the stream while they're watching us, being careful not to get their lips (all sugar, of course) wet. He guesses that their 'blood' must be almost pure water, and that it washes away (from the inside, of course) the sugar they need for energy. I asked him where the sugar came from, and he said probably their bodies isolated carbon from something (he thought it might be the moss) and combined it with the hydrogen and oxygen in the water (even I knew the formula for water) to make sugar, a common carbohydrate.

units.claim: Kroger compared the Martians' process to plant photosynthesis but using the shape of scales to isolate necessary spectra.
units.evidence: Like plants, on Earth, he said. Except, instead of using special cells on leaves to form carbohydrates with the help of sunpower, as Earth plants do in photosynthesis (Kroger spelled that word for me), they used the shape of the scales like prisms, to isolate the spectra (another Kroger word) necessary to form the sugar.

units.claim: Kroger explained that the Martians fear water because it dissolves their energy source and alters the shape of their scales.
units.evidence: Simple, he said, as though he were addressing me by name. They have a twofold reason to fear water. One: by complete solvency in that medium, they lose all energy and die. Two: even partial sprinkling alters the shape of the scales, and they are unable to use sunpower to form more sugar, and still die, if a bit slower.
